bio.en: Bob Baxley is a designer and executive who built and led design teams at Apple, Pinterest, Yahoo, and ThoughtSpot over a three-decade career, shaping products used by hundreds of millions.
bio.zh: Bob Baxley 是一位设计师和高管，在三十年的职业生涯中于 Apple、Pinterest、Yahoo 和 ThoughtSpot 构建并领导设计团队，塑造了数亿人使用的产品。

summary.en: Bob offers a unique perspective that design is “imagining the future you want to live in and taking steps to make it real,” and that being design-led is different from being designer-led. He reflects on why Apple's design DNA had to be present from the start and the lessons of witnessing history there. The conversation covers why product people have an obligation to put positive emotional energy back into people's lives and how to build a lasting design culture.
summary.zh: Bob 提出独特观点：设计是“想象你想生活的未来，并采取措施使之成真”，且“设计驱动”不同于“设计师驱动”。他反思了为何 Apple 的设计基因必须从一开始就存在，以及在那里见证历史的教训。对话涵盖为何产品人有义务把积极的情感能量归还给用户生活，以及如何建立持久的设计文化。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Almost everyone living in a modern economy now is going to have hundreds of interactions with a phone or with a computer. And unfortunately, a lot of those interactions are not going to be great. We have an obligation as product people to put that emotional energy back into people's lives.
turns.zh: 如今，几乎每个生活在现代经济体系中的人都会与手机或电脑产生数百次互动。遗憾的是，其中许多互动体验并不理想。作为产品从业者，我们有责任为人们的生活注入更多情感能量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You actually have a really unique perspective on just what is design.
turns.zh: 你对设计的理解确实独到。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Design is trying to imagine the future you want to live in and then take the steps to make it real. Saying a company is design-led does not mean it's designer-led. I've never seen somebody graft it on after the fact. It's there at the beginning in the root DNA or doesn't exist. (00:00:31): It wasn't a successful stint at Pinterest. I just bounced off the culture. I came in thinking I was supposed to behave the way I behaved at Apple, which is very direct, fighting hard.
turns.zh: 设计意味着构想你理想中的未来生活，并采取行动将其变为现实。说一家公司以设计为导向，并不等于说它由设计师主导。我从未见过哪个公司是事后才强行引入设计思维的。这种理念要么根植于创立之初的基因里，要么根本不存在。（00:00:31）我在Pinterest的经历并不成功。我与那里的文化格格不入。我刚加入时还以为自己应该沿用在苹果养成的处事风格——直言不讳、勇于抗争。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why did you decide to join Apple?
turns.zh: 你为什么决定加入苹果？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: I just seek out opportunities to witness history. The whole company is constantly asking how can the thing that I'm working on be a little bit better?
turns.zh: 我始终在寻找见证历史的机会。整个公司都在不断追问：我所负责的项目如何能再往前迈进一步？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Lenny, thank you so much. Thanks for having me, but also just thank you for what you do. We are still in early days to try to figure out how to make software together. I think of it like where the film industry was in the 1920s. We've had our talkie moment. We're on the cusp of having our shift to color movement, but we're still trying to figure out how to make movies and a podcast like yours specifically yours I think is one of the greatest resources we have for learning from one another. I appreciate all you're doing for the community and for helping us as a community make better software.
turns.zh: 莱尼，非常感谢你。我很感激你邀请我来访，同时也感谢你所做的一切。我们仍处于探索如何共同开发软件的初期阶段。我觉得这就像1920年代的电影业。我们曾经历过有声电影的时代，如今正处于向彩色电影转型的前夜，但我们仍在摸索如何制作电影——而像你这样的播客，无疑是我们相互学习的最佳资源之一。我赞赏你为社区所做的一切，也感激你帮助我们共同打造更优质的软件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Well, I really appreciate that. That means a lot coming from you. There's so much I want to talk about in our conversation. There's a story that I hear that you often tell, which is when somebody asked Steve Jobs once, what is your favorite product that you've built that you work on? And his answer, what's that story?
turns.zh: 哇。嗯，真的很感激你这么说。这对我意义非凡。在我们的对话中，有很多想聊的话题。我听过你常讲的一个故事，讲的是有人问史蒂夫·乔布斯，你最引以为傲的产品是什么？他的回答是什么？这个故事是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: So I actually can't remember where I heard this, but I believe the story's true. Steve at one point was recounting the products that he had created that he was most proud of, and if I recall the whole list, it was the Apple II, the Mac, the iPod, the iPhone, I think Apple retail was in the list and then he said Apple itself. When I heard that and when I've reflected on it, that is the longest lasting thing. I remember there was also a story that Steve was talking to, I think it was either Ed Catmull or John Lasseter at Pixar, and he said, "Everything we make is going to be a doorstop in three years, but the stuff you guys make, they're still going to be watching in 100 years." So I think Steve had some concept of the longevity of these things. (00:05:33): They knew the products themselves were very ephemeral, but there's something about the culture of Apple that's lasted a very long time and I personally believe will last for some time yet to come. It's a way of making decisions, it's a way of behaving, it's a way of seeing the value of technology in the world and it infuses everything in that company. I mean everything from the checkout system when you go to the receptionist to what it's like in the cafeteria. At least when I was there, they had patented the pizza box because they had reinvented the pizza box that you would get at Cafe Max because the whole company is constantly asking how can the thing that I'm working on be a little bit better? I think that was something Steve brought to them and had them constantly asking that question.
turns.zh: 其实我记不清是在哪里听说的，但我相信这个故事是真实的。史蒂夫曾列举他最自豪的几款产品，如果我没记错的话，名单包括Apple II、Mac、iPod、iPhone，还有苹果零售店。然后他说苹果本身也是他引以为豪的。听到这个故事后，我深有感触。最持久的影响是什么？我记得还有一个故事，史蒂夫和皮克斯的埃德·卡特穆尔或约翰·拉塞特交谈时，他说：“我们做的东西三年后都会成为门挡，但你们做的作品，100年后人们还会在看。” 所以我认为史蒂夫对这些产品的持久性有深刻认识。他们知道产品本身很短暂，但苹果的文化却经久不衰。我个人相信这种文化还会延续很久。这是一种决策方式、行为准则，也是看待科技价值的视角，它渗透在公司的方方面面——从前台接待处的收银系统，到食堂的环境。至少我在那里时，他们为披萨盒申请了专利，因为他们重新发明了Cafe Max那种披萨盒。整个公司都在不断追问：我正在做的这件事能否再好一点？我认为这是史蒂夫灌输给他们的理念，让他们始终保持这种质疑精神。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One more Apple question then I'll move on to other stuff. Why do you think that people that have left Apple, a lot of amazing things haven't emerged from people that have left? Humane was a recent example. We're recording this the day after Jony Ive Open AI emerged so we'll see what happens there but just feels like there hasn't been a ton of alumni that have built incredible things.
turns.zh: 再问一个关于苹果的问题，然后我们再聊其他的。你觉得为什么那么多离开苹果的人都没有创造出惊艳的成果？Humane就是最近的一个例子。我们录制这期节目的时候，乔纳森·伊夫刚加入OpenAI，所以让我们拭目以待，但总体感觉离开苹果的校友中没有太多能创造出非凡成果的。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Obviously Tony Fadell would be one with Nest and he'd be an outlier. I think the people that... I went to Pinterest and did not have a successful time in my year and a half at Pinterest. I think my own particular mistake, and I've seen this with some other Apple executives as well as we went directly from Apple, I left Apple on a Friday and I started Pinterest on a Monday. I didn't give myself time to recalibrate to the Pinterest culture. I think at some level, a lot of the challenge is that Apple, and it's not just Apple, I think every major tech company, they have really powerful cultures. (00:07:11): You get indoctrinated into all those standards and it's really deep. It fuses all of your behavior and how you conduct yourself in the company, away from the company. I think it's pretty hard to immigrate successfully from one of those environments to another. Apple is one of the strongest cultures and there's not many other cultures that natively operate like that. Airbnb is one exception. And so you have guys like Hiroki Asai who leads all of marketing and all of product and Hiroki is crushing at Airbnb. He was incredibly successful at Apple. (00:07:43): It also should be noted that he had, it was a multi-year gap between the time he left Apple and the time he started Airbnb. He gave himself a little bit of time to get through the... At Apple, I think it was Tim or Steve used to talk about the Apple car wash. Then when you started Apple, they kind of had to take you through the car wash and get off all that stuff that you'd accumulated at other places. It turns out there's a car wash you need to go through when you leave Apple as well. And so I think Hiroki gave himself time to do that and I think that's probably a lot of why he's been so successful at Airbnb. The thing I took away from Apple, and I think this is true for anybody changing from one major culture to another is most likely the new place hires you because of the values of the organization you left, but not the behaviors. (00:08:23): And so I think it's important to recalibrate and say, well, I want to hold onto these values. So at Apple, attention to detail, product excellence, doing everything you can for the customer and the user so try to hold onto those values but then think, okay, how are those values best expressed in this culture? I was more successful at expressing those values in the culture of ThoughtSpot, which was my last job than I was in the culture of Pinterest. If I had to do it again, I could probably do better at Pinterest. I think that's useful for anybody leaving one very specific culture and going someplace else, try to hold onto the values but not the behaviors.
turns.zh: 显然，托尼·法德尔（Tony Fadell）在Nest的经历是个例外。我认为那些……我去Pinterest工作，但在那里的一年半时间里并不成功。我认为我自己犯了错误，我也观察到其他苹果高管也有同样的问题。我们直接从苹果离职，周五离开苹果，周一就开始在Pinterest工作。我没有给自己时间去适应Pinterest的文化。我认为在某种程度上，挑战在于苹果——不只是苹果，每家大型科技公司都有非常强大的文化。（00:07:11）：你会被灌输所有那些标准，而且这种影响非常深刻。它渗透到你所有的行为举止中，无论是在公司内还是在公司外。我认为从其中一种环境成功迁移到另一种环境非常困难。苹果的文化是最强的，没有多少其他文化能像它那样天生运作。Airbnb是个例外。所以像浅井宏树（Hiroki Asai）这样的人，负责市场和产品部门，他在Airbnb表现出色。他在苹果时也非常成功。（00:07:43）：还值得注意的是，他离开苹果和开始Airbnb之间有几年的间隔。他给自己一些时间去适应……在苹果，蒂姆（Tim）或史蒂夫（Steve）常提到的"苹果洗车"环节。然后当你加入苹果时，他们会带你经历一个"洗车"过程，清除你在其他地方积累的那些东西。结果发现，当你离开苹果时，也需要经历一个"洗车"过程。所以我认为宏树给自己时间去做这件事，这很可能是他在Airbnb如此成功的原因之一。我从苹果带走的东西，我认为这对任何从一种主要文化转向另一种文化的人都是适用的，最有可能的是新公司因为你离开的公司的价值观而雇用你，而不是行为方式。（00:08:23）：所以我认为重要的是要重新调整心态，说，好吧，我想坚持这些价值观。所以在苹果，注重细节、产品卓越、尽一切可能为客户和用户服务，试着坚持这些价值观，但然后想一想，在这种文化中如何最好地表达这些价值观？我在上一个工作ThoughtSpot的文化中比在Pinterest的文化中更成功地表达了这些价值观。如果我能再来一次，我可能会在Pinterest做得更好。对于任何离开一种特定文化去其他地方的人，我认为试着坚持价值观而不是行为方式是很有用的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting and I appreciate you sharing that, the way you described it that it wasn't a successful stint at Pinterest. A lot of people don't share that sort of story and don't put it that way. They see on their LinkedIn, oh, a head of design at Pinterest. Oh, amazing so cool. And then if you're like, oh, okay, but it didn't work out that well, I think that's really interesting. Is there anything more you can share there about what you learned for other people to maybe avoid that sort of situation? Anything you took away from that experience?
turns.zh: 这太有趣了，感谢你分享这些经历。你描述在Pinterest工作并不成功，这真的很有意思。很多人不会分享这种经历，也不会这样说出来。他们在领英上看到，哦，Pinterest的首席设计师。哦，太棒了，太酷了。然后如果你说哦，好吧，但结果并不理想，我觉得这真的很有意思。你能否分享更多你从中吸取的教训，让其他人或许能避免这种情况？你从这次经历中得到了什么启发？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: One of my friends that was at Pinterest, I'm still friends with, he said, "I just thought of it as you bounced off the culture." I think that's kind of the way to think of it. I came in thinking I was supposed to behave the way I behaved at Apple, which is very direct, fighting hard. Everybody cares about each other. It's never insulting, but it's intense. That's not really where Pinterest was at the time. Again, all this is a decade ago, so I don't know what any of these companies are like today, but at least when I was there, Pinterest had posters in every conference room that said, big poster that said, say the hard thing. Well, that's where Pinterest was at the time, and I can assure you nobody at Apple was having to remind you to say the hard thing. (00:10:07): And so I probably could have picked up on that better than I did. I'll say these careers are really hard and the higher up you go, people think of it like you're climbing a pyramid. I think of it more like you're going out on a branch on a tree and the branch gets a lot more flimsy and can break and you can fall and you get buffeted about by the wind. It's often at a time in your life when there's a lot going on with your family, there could be things going on with your parents' health. I lost my mother when I was at Pinterest. My kids were starting high school, so we're struggling with the teenage years. I had a long commute. It's a lot going on and these jobs are super demanding. (00:10:46): Everything around you is changing really rapidly and you're under tremendous pressure because the financial and success stakes are super high. I think the people falling off of these jobs is the common use case. That is the common story. We have a bias towards survivors and we all talk about how it looks like they made it to the top, but everybody that makes it to the top, there's hundreds of people that don't. One of the things I took away when I was at Pinterest was I came to think that the job of a startup was to grow the founder so they could continue to lead the startup. I think what's true for founders, also true for a lot of the other folks in the executive staff, it's very hard to grow emotionally and developmentally at the rate that the company grows. (00:11:32): A lot of times I think people get outgrown by the role, and I saw that across Apple. I've experienced that myself at different times in my career. I see that happening with my friends and it feels like a failure. I mean, that is the human experience, that's what happens. It's very hard to grow as fast as some of these companies are growing and we could debate the merits of Mark Zuckerberg for example. But when you think about the trajectory from being a kid in a dorm room to within five years, Facebook's a big thing. I mean, think of your own life. Can you process that level of evolution and change? I don't know, I think that's really super hard to do that and stay balanced.
turns.zh: 我在Pinterest的一位朋友，现在仍是我的好友。他曾说：“我当时觉得你只是被那里的文化压得喘不过气了。” 我觉得这就是个很好的理解方式。我刚加入时以为自己应该延续在苹果养成的行事风格——直言不讳、拼命争取。大家互相关心，从不互相攻击，但竞争十分激烈。但当时的Pinterest显然不是这样的。再说了，这都是十年前的事了，所以我不知道这些公司如今是什么样子，但至少在我待在那里时，每个会议室都挂着大幅标语，写着“说出难听的话”。当时的Pinterest就是这样，我可以向你保证，在苹果公司可没人需要提醒你要说出难听的话。（00:10:07）所以我本该更敏锐地察觉到这一点。我想说，这些职业生涯真的很艰难，职位越高，人们就越觉得自己在攀登金字塔。我更倾向于把它比作在树枝上攀爬——树枝越往上越脆弱，随时可能折断，你会被狂风吹得东摇西摆。通常，这时候你的家庭会面临诸多变故，比如父母健康问题。当我在Pinterest时，母亲去世了。我的孩子们刚上高中，正值青春叛逆期。通勤时间又很长。种种压力叠加，再加上这些工作的高强度要求。（00:10:46）你周围的一切都在飞速变化，巨大的财务和成功压力压得你喘不过气。我认为从这些岗位上倒下的人才是常态。这才是常见的职业轨迹。我们总偏爱那些成功者，总说他们似乎轻易登顶，但每个登顶者背后，都有成百上千个未能成功的人。我在Pinterest最大的收获是意识到初创公司的职责应该是培养创始人，让他们能持续领导公司。我认为这对创始人适用，对高管团队中的许多人同样适用——要想在情感和成长上跟上公司的步伐实在太难了。（00:11:32）很多时候，人们会被职位压得喘不过气，我在苹果也见过这种情况。我自己职业生涯中也多次经历过。我看到朋友们深受其害，这感觉像是一种失败。我的意思是，这就是人性，这就是必然会发生的事。要想跟上某些公司的发展速度，实在太难了。我们可以讨论马克·扎克伯格的优点，但当你回想从宿舍少年到五年内创立Facebook的轨迹时，再想想自己的生活，能否承受这样的进化和变革速度？我不知道，我觉得要做到这点并保持平衡实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also keep doing that for so long. There'll be founders, I think it was Brian's maybe first job or second job, and he's doing that now for 15 years in a row.
turns.zh: 而且还要长期坚持这样做。我记得布莱恩可能是他的第一份或第二份工作，而他现在已经连续15年做着同样的事了。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Oh, founders, it's their life. It's very unusual to see founders move out. I had this other theory that a startup is still a startup until the founder moves aside. By my definition of even Meta is still a startup in a way that Amazon's not, and Airbnb is still a startup in a way that Pinterest is not because Ben's moved on. You don't find out if the culture can sustain itself until the founders are gone and then you really see what's going to happen.
turns.zh: 哦，各位创始人啊，这毕竟是他们的生活。创始人离职的情况实属罕见。我曾有过另一种观点——只要创始人还未退出舞台，初创公司就始终是初创公司。按照我的定义，即便Facebook（Meta）已然上市，但在某种程度上，它仍像亚马逊一样是初创公司；而Airbnb（爱彼家）也比Pinterest（拼趣）更具初创属性，因为本·西尔伯曼（Ben Silbermann）已另谋高就。要等到创始人离开后，你才能真正判断企业文化能否自我延续——到那时，你才会见证未来会发生什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to close the loop here, one takeaway here that I think is really interesting is that you can fail in a job and things will be okay. Clearly you're doing A okay and having a place that doesn't work out, doesn't destroy your career, which I think a lot of people feel like if they're not doing well in their current job, it's over. Things are all going to go downhill
turns.zh: 最后再总结一下，这里有个非常有趣的启示：工作上的失败未必意味着人生完蛋。显然，你在A公司的工作表现出色，即便遭遇职场挫折，也不至于葬送职业生涯。我发现很多人都误以为，只要当前工作不顺，一切就都完蛋了，然后就陷入悲观情绪。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Your career's not your life. There's a lot more to it than that.
turns.zh: 职业生涯毕竟不是全部生活，远不止于此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then just to give someone something tactical here, so you've realized the culture of Pinterest, you bounced off of it. I love that metaphor. If you were to, when you're looking at new companies, what's one thing you look at or a question you ask or something you now look at to make sure you avoid that in the future, that culture clash?
turns.zh: 再给点实用建议：既然你已经深刻理解了Pinterest的企业文化并从中抽身而出，我很欣赏这种隐喻。当你考察新公司时，怎样避免文化冲突？你会关注哪些方面？会提出哪些问题？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: I'm fortunate at this stage of my career that I usually get to interview with the CEO or the founders or something like that. What I'm usually looking for is do they have a story as to why they believe in design? Really in their heart and soul, do they care about design? Because if I go into a company that doesn't really value the thing that I do, I'm just not going to have a great time and I'm going to be constantly buffeting up against all sorts of people. I want to make sure I've got air cover from the highest people in the company setting the culture. (00:13:57): In the case of, again, my most recent job was with a company called ThoughtSpot. And ThoughtSpot was founded by a gentleman named Ajeet Singh, and Ajeet grew up in rural India, but he tells this really great story about he studied chemical engineering, he moves to the United States. Early in his career, he's working for Honeywell and they did a couple of engagements with IDEO. As a very young person, he got to see what IDEO did and he realized the power of design and he's taken that to all of his companies. He started Nutanix before he came to ThoughtSpot, before he started ThoughtSpot. And so when I heard that, I'm like, oh, this is a guy that gets design right from the very beginning. (00:14:32): I've also come to believe that I actually have never seen a company that grafted design on after the founding. I could name lots of companies that I think are kind of design led, not always designer led, but design led or design centric. But I've never seen somebody grafted on after the fact. It's there at the beginning in the root DNA or doesn't exist. And so the thing that I'm looking for when I interview is, is it there at the beginning? Can I get a credible story that tracks it back to that? (00:14:59): And if that's the case, then I think I can find a way to navigate in that culture. We have a shared value system in a way that as an American, I could immigrate to Australia and the culture would be slightly different, but we'd have a shared value system that I could relate to. If I moved to, I don't know, Burma or China or something, it would be wildly more challenging because the base view of the world, the base understanding of the world's just different and it'd be much harder for me to adapt to that.
turns.zh: 在我职业生涯的现阶段，我很幸运能有机会与CEO、创始人或类似高层进行面试。我通常想了解的是，他们是否有关于为何相信设计的深刻见解？他们内心深处是否真正在乎设计？因为如果我进入一家不重视我所从事工作的公司，我注定不会有好的体验，还会不断与各种人产生摩擦。我需要确保公司最高层能为我营造支持性的文化环境。（00:13:57）：以我最近的工作经历为例，我加入的ThoughtSpot公司由Ajeet Singh创立。他在印度农村长大，但讲述了一个精彩的故事——他曾学习化学工程，后来移居美国。职业生涯早期，他在霍尼韦尔工作，参与过IDEO的多个项目。年少时，他目睹了IDEO的成果，意识到设计的力量，并将这种理念贯穿于他创立的所有公司。在加入ThoughtSpot之前，他还创立了Nutanix公司。听完这些，我意识到这是一个从一开始就把设计理念融入血液的创始人。（00:14:32）：我还发现，创始人后续强行添加设计元素的公司凤毛麟角。我能列举出许多看似以设计为导向的公司（不一定由设计师主导），但很少有公司是在创立后才追加设计的。设计理念要么根植于初创阶段，要么根本不存在。因此面试时我会关注：设计理念是否从一开始就融入血液？能否找到可靠的逻辑线将其追溯至初创时期？（00:14:59）：如果答案是肯定的，那么我就能找到在这种文化中航行的方法。就像美国人移居澳大利亚，文化差异虽有，但价值观体系相通；若移居缅甸或中国等国，文化冲击将远超想象，因为世界观与理解方式存在根本差异，适应难度极大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a way to extrapolate that insight is just whatever function you're in, get a sense of how important that function is to that business. Do the founders value engineering? Do they value product? Do they value design? Depending on who you are.
turns.zh: 我认为深化这一洞察的关键在于：无论你身处何种职位，都要了解该职能对公司的核心价值。创始人重视工程吗？重视产品吗？重视设计吗？这取决于你的角色。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Why would you want to work in a place that doesn't value the thing that you do? God, that would suck.
turns.zh: 为何要选择一个不重视你所做之事的公司？天哪，那简直太糟糕了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You actually have a really unique perspective on just what is design that I haven't heard before. Let me ask you that question is what is design?
turns.zh: 你对设计的定义真是独到，我从未听过如此深刻的见解。让我再问你一个问题：什么是设计？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, I'm going to go back to the Edward Tufte quote that I use all the time, which is design is clear thinking made visible. And so I think most people when they talk about design, they think of it as the visual expression of an idea. They think of it as a team or a function or a group. I think of it as a holistic mindset. When design thinking became big, I was always really confused because I didn't know how else you could think. That was just how I naturally thought, which is design is trying to imagine the future you want to live in and then take the steps to make it real. (00:16:27): It's living with a certain type of intentionality in almost a Buddhist type way, which is different from science, which is observational trying to understand. It's a little bit different from engineering, which is we kind of know where we want go at the end, but we're trying to go one step at a time versus design's trying to see some further out future state and account for a larger or a different set of constraints and issues than engineering or some of the other problem solving methodologies. Again, I look at it as a company, does the company think in a design mindset and Apple does, Airbnb does. I don't get the sense that Google does and I don't get the sense that Amazon does. That's not a critique on them. I don't think that those organizations are competing on design in the same way. But again, I want to go work at a place that as an organization thinks in a design type method.
turns.zh: 好吧，我要再回顾一下我经常引用的爱德华·塔夫特（Edward Tufte）的一句话：设计就是清晰的思维具象化。因此，我认为大多数人谈论设计时，都将其视为某个想法的视觉表达。他们把设计看作一个团队、一项职能或一个群体。但对我而言，设计是一种整体思维模式。当设计思维兴起时，我曾深感困惑，因为我实在不明白还能用其他方式思考。对我而言，设计就是努力构想你理想中的未来生活，然后采取行动将其变为现实。（00:16:27）这就像以佛家般的专注力去生活，与科学的观察式理解有所不同，也与工程学有所区别——工程学是我们大致知道最终目标，但按部就班地推进；而设计则试图展望更远的未来状态，并考量比工程学或其他问题解决方法更广泛、更复杂的约束条件与挑战。再说回企业层面，我观察到苹果和爱彼迎都秉持设计思维，而谷歌和亚马逊似乎并非如此。这并非对他们的批评——我认为这些公司在设计方面的竞争策略本质不同。但我渴望加入那种以设计思维为核心理念的组织。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, a lot of people imagine every founder, every product builder is just, yes, I'd love amazing design. I'd love our products to be incredibly beautiful, intuitive, so easy for everyone to use and understand, but they don't actually invest in these areas and they don't put a lot of resources into the designing process. What's the best pitch you can make and that you do make to companies to help them see the strategic value of design and the bottom of the value of design.
turns.zh: 基于此，许多人误以为每位创业者、产品开发者都心想：没错，我渴望卓越的设计，渴望产品美观易用、直观易懂。但现实是，他们并未真正投入这些领域，也未为设计流程注入充足资源。请问，您向企业推销设计价值时，最有效的切入点是什么？如何让他们深刻认识到设计的战略意义和商业价值？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Let me back up and just dissect a little bit the way you described design, you described it in really tactical terms. You said beautiful, intuitive products that make sense. I think it was something like that. What you were describing was you were describing the part of the iceberg that sits above the water line, which is the result. That's one of the outcomes of design, but that's not the real heavy lifting of design. Design is more like liberal arts or philosophy or something. It's like what do we try to achieve at a much lower level? And so what I talk to founders and people about the value of design, what I'm pushing them on is when we can get organizational alignment around what we want to do philosophically, why do we exist? What's the vision for the company? How do all these things ladder up through vision, through mission, through specific tenets, design strategies. (00:18:36): And then into actual execution. How do we ladder that whole thing up so it makes sense as a whole? That's the magic of design. The difference is when you design things, you end up with a bunch of bricks that are piled into a beautiful impenetrable wall. If you don't do that, you end up with a bunch of bricks scattered across the backyard and they don't really add up to anything. I think that's one of the things, if you look, again to go back to Apple, but we could also talk about Lego Lyca, Porsche, Airbnb, Patagonia, there's other companies that make sense as a design centered organization. If you think about everything they do, it all ladders together into one cohesive sensical thing. It's integrated. Makes sense as a unit. (00:19:20): I think that's a huge difference and an incredible strategic advantage because the company can operate with much greater efficiency. They can onboard new people and get them in line. Even Apple, for example, the team that designed the online store, we had six designers for a store that ran in 30 some odd countries, 12 and a half thousand instances of the store doing billions of dollars of revenue. We had six designers. Any other company would've had 60 or more. Apple's able to operate with much smaller staff because they have real clarity of vision of what they're doing. And the benefit of operating with a smaller staff is not just that it saves money on payroll, it's that you have... The way the minds come together to create something that feels like a single whole is a much higher chance when you have fewer people involved. (00:20:10): I joke about The Beatles. You get The Beatles with four people, you don't get The Beatles with eight people and you certainly don't get it with 24 people. The teams get too big and you can't get that what Brian Eno calls scenius. Brian Eno has this great word that he uses, scenius is the genius that comes when you have a group together. Scenius is the collective idea of genius and I think that's something that's really magical that I've experienced in my career, but usually in smaller groups. It's hard to do with a giant group.
turns.zh:
让我先回过头来，仔细拆解一下你对设计的描述。你用了非常务实的词汇来形容设计，比如“美观、直观、易懂的产品”。我想大概是这样的。你所描述的只是冰山露出水面的一部分，也就是最终的成果。这只是设计的成果之一，但并非设计的核心工作。设计更像是人文学科或哲学。它更像是在更深层次上要达成什么目标？所以当我向创始人和其他人谈论设计的价值时，我会追问他们：我们能否在组织层面达成一致，明确我们在哲学层面想要做什么？公司的愿景是什么？这些理念如何通过愿景、使命和具体原则、设计策略层层递进，最终形成一个整体？这才是设计的魔力。关键在于，当你设计产品时，最终得到的是一堵用砖块砌成的坚不可摧的墙。如果不这样做，砖块就会散落在后院，毫无章法。

我认为这就是关键所在。以苹果为例，但我们也可以谈谈乐高、保时捷、爱彼家、巴塔哥尼亚等公司。这些以设计为核心的组织，其一切行动都紧密相连，浑然一体。它们是整合的。作为一个整体，逻辑清晰。

（00:18:36）：这就是巨大的差异，也是令人惊叹的战略优势，因为公司能够以更高的效率运作。他们能更快地吸纳新人并让他们跟上节奏。以苹果为例，设计在线商店的团队只有六个人，而这个商店在30多个国家运营，拥有1.25万个实例，每年创造数十亿美元的收入。其他公司可能需要60人甚至更多。苹果能用更少的人员运作，是因为他们对目标有清晰的愿景。更少人员的好处不仅在于节省薪资成本，还在于当参与人数较少时，人们的思维更容易凝聚成一个整体。

（00:20:10）：我常拿披头士乐队打比方。四个人的披头士是披头士，八个人就不是了，更别说24个人了。团队规模过大，便无法获得布莱恩·伊诺所说的"天才群"。布莱恩·伊诺创造了一个词"天才群"，指的是当一群人聚在一起时产生的集体智慧。我在职业生涯中就经历过这种神奇的效果，但通常是在较小的团队里。在大型团队中很难实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this metaphor of The Beatles as the way most people describe this is designed by committee never works. I love that the way you describe it is the Beatles is like the ideal size a small group versus a committee.
turns.zh: 我喜欢用披头士乐队这个比喻，因为大多数人描述的"委员会式设计"从来都行不通。我喜欢你用披头士来比喻，说明小团队比委员会式的设计更理想。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: I just always have to point out to people that there are 20 people that worked on the original Mac. I mean it's 20 of them, that's it, 20. Susan Kare was one of them, Andy Hertzfeld, you go through the list, 20 of them are on the patent. There's 24 that are on the iPhone patent. Now there's other people involved, but generally there's 24 people on the iPhone patent. And that was the team. That was Project Purple that was doing that stuff. These are not massive massive groups doing these things. If you had put a massive group, I don't know man, maybe it'd end up with the Zune or something completely different. Who knows?
turns.zh: 我总是要提醒人们，原始Mac团队有20个人参与开发。我的意思是，确实是20个人，仅此而已，20个人。苏珊·卡尔（Susan Kare）是其中之一，安迪·赫茨菲尔德（Andy Hertzfeld）也是。你把名单列出来，20个人在专利上署名。iPhone专利上有24个人。当然还有其他参与者，但总的来说，iPhone专利共有24个人。这就是当时的团队——那个负责项目的团队"紫色计划"（Project Purple）。这并非庞大的团队。如果当时组建一个庞大的团队，我不知道结果会怎样，也许最后会搞出个Zune之类完全不同的产品，谁知道呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They probably did have a massive group on the Zune.
turns.zh: 他们在Zune项目上可能确实组建了庞大的团队。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, so there's something, four is too few for what we're trying to achieve at scale. But even if you look at Pixar, any good movie on the scripting and story side, it's usually a fairly small team. Even when you move into character development, stuff like that, it's fairly small and then it really scales when you move into production. It's just hard to figure out something new to do together when there's too many people involved.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以对于我们想要大规模实现的目标来说，四个人确实太少了。但即便看看皮克斯（Pixar），任何一部优秀电影在剧本创作和故事构思方面，都通常由一个相当小的团队完成。即使进入角色开发等阶段，团队规模也相当小，而真正大规模化是在制作阶段。这就是为什么当涉及太多人时，很难一起想出新点子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that word new is really key here. I think when people hear this advice, they're thinking at their existing company, should we just keep our company small? Should we not scale this thing that we have? I think what you're describing, which I completely agree with is new stuff for sure you want to keep the team small and tight, but as things grow and scale, what's your take on just, okay, actually it's okay to have a lot of people on this.
turns.zh: 我认为“新”这个词在这里很关键。我觉得当人们听到这个建议时，他们会想到自己现有的公司，应该保持公司规模小吗？我们是否不应该扩大现有规模？我完全同意你的观点，新项目确实需要保持团队规模小而紧凑，但随着项目发展和规模扩大，多人参与又未尝不可。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, you have to bring a lot of people in once you figure out what you're doing. And so to your point, once you realize you're building Disneyland and you've got the whole thing set and people know what it's about, then they can come in and understand, oh, I'm playing my piece over here. I'm supposed to design the line experience for the new ride sitting in Tomorrowland, but I know where that fits into this larger thing. I think you can scale once you have clarity of vision, but it's very difficult to get vision with a lot of people.
turns.zh: 嗯，一旦你确定了要做什么，就必须引入大量人才。正如你所说，当你意识到自己在建造迪士尼乐园，整个项目已经规划妥当，人们也明白了其核心理念时，他们就能加入进来，理解自己该做什么。例如，我要为明日世界的新游乐设施设计排队体验，但我知道这在整个项目中处于什么位置。一旦有了清晰的愿景，规模扩展就容易多了，但当团队人数众多时，要形成清晰的愿景却非常困难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. I think that's really powerful advice. It's just when you're starting something new. I actually had a CPA of N26 who was basically leading Google Hangouts, the initial launch of Google Hangouts, and he told the story of they put so many resources on it. We got to win. We got to do this. Larry Page or Sergey was sitting next to him just like we got to make this work and putting everything they could into it and it didn't work out. And I think that's-
turns.zh: 太好了。我认为这确实是很有价值的建议。只是当你刚开始做新项目时。我曾接触过N26的首席财务官，他当时负责谷歌环聊（Google Hangouts）的初期发布。他讲述了他们投入大量资源的故事。我们必须成功。我们必须做到这一点。拉里·佩奇（Larry Page）或谢尔盖·布林（Sergey）就坐在他旁边，强调必须让这个项目成功，全力以赴，但最终还是失败了。我认为这说明——

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: No, no, the more people you put in it, the slower everything becomes.
turns.zh: 不，不，不，多人参与只会让一切进展得更慢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to go back to something you said about what design is. I think this is really interesting. And so the way you described design to a lot of people, it sounds like that's like product management also and product leadership, setting, strategy, vision, figuring out how everything fits together. I think your experience here, I think Apple is a very different kind of company where design actually leads a lot of this. At a lot of other companies, it doesn't work that way. Any thoughts? And just how you advise companies, think about the split between design and product management that aren't Apple.
turns.zh: 我想回到你之前关于设计是什么的论点。我觉得这非常有趣。你向很多人描述设计时，听起来这就像产品管理和产品领导力——制定战略、愿景，协调各部分关系。我认为你在苹果公司的经历很有启发，因为苹果确实让设计主导了许多工作流程。但在其他很多公司，情况并非如此。你有什么看法吗？还有，你如何建议那些非苹果公司的公司去处理设计与产品管理的分工问题？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: One of the best lines I ever heard was from my friend Joseph O'Sullivan at dinner one night. He said saying a company is design led does not mean it's designer led. And so what I try to hammer home with people is that when I talk about design as a mindset, I'm talking about it as a mindset. Anybody could have that mindset functioning in any role, any designer could have a product mindset. In fact, I think that's a lot of what the design community is trying to get at now when they say designers should be speaking the language of business. I think what they're saying is designers need to inhabit the product mindset as well. Maybe to some degree even the sales mindset. (00:24:11): Look, both functions matter. I look at my counterparts in product and I assume that they're much better connected to the customer, that they understand much better the business realities, and I expect them to drive the roadmap. I may have some points of view on the roadmap. I may offer some critique. I may have my own suggestions and agenda in there. But once they say this is the roadmap, I have to believe that they're right and I don't try to bleed into their space. I very much believe that once you get into a company, your job is to figure out your role and respect the boundaries between the different groups. (00:24:43): I'm like, you guys tell us what you need us to do, what the features need to be, when they need to be delivered, what the issues are, and then give us the time and space to come up with a solution to those problems. And then we can work together to decide whether or not our solutions actually solve the problem as you understand it, but I'll stay out of your roadmap and you stay out of my design stop and let's try to get to the promised land together. I assume that the product managers, particularly in enterprise SaaS companies, like my team, ThoughtSpot did data analytics. My team didn't know anything about data analytics. We didn't have any of that insight. We didn't have the bandwidth, the mental horsepower to go out and do that stuff. We had our hands full just trying to figure out the UI. (00:25:22): It's one of the points I try to make too, when people are starting to theorize that gen AI can remove teammates and oh, the designers don't need engineers and the PMs don't need the designers and everybody thinks they can throw engineering overboard. And I'm like, stop it. We all need each other and we need each other because we need those different mindsets. One of those mindsets inhabits somebody's head completely. I just don't think you can simultaneously hold multiple mindsets in your head. It's not that one of my PM counterparts couldn't bring a lot to the design table, it's just I need you to play that position. Like in baseball, the second-
turns.zh: 我听过最精彩的一句话来自我的朋友约瑟夫·奥沙利文，一次晚餐时他说道："说公司是设计主导的，并不意味着设计师主导。"所以我反复向人们强调，当我谈到设计是一种思维模式时，我指的确实是一种思维模式。任何人都能具备这种思维模式，任何设计师都能拥有产品思维。事实上，我认为这正是当下设计界正努力达成的目标——设计师应该学会用商业语言交流。我认为他们真正想说的是，设计师也需要具备产品思维，甚至在某种程度上还要具备销售思维。（00:24:11）：看，两种职能都很重要。我观察产品团队的同事，认为他们与客户的联系更紧密，更能理解商业现实，我期望他们主导路线图规划。我可能会对路线图提出一些看法，也许会提出批评意见，提出自己的建议和主张。但一旦他们确定了路线图，我必须相信他们的判断，不试图越界。我坚信，一旦进入公司，你的工作就是明确自己的角色，尊重不同团队之间的界限。（00:24:43）：我会说：你们告诉我们需要做什么，功能需求是什么，交付时间是什么，问题在哪里。然后给我们时间和空间去解决这些问题。之后我们可以一起判断我们的解决方案是否真正解决了你们理解的问题，但我不会干涉你们的路线图，你们也不要干涉我的设计工作。比如在企业级SaaS公司，像我的团队ThoughtSpot做数据分析时，我的团队对数据分析一无所知。我们没有任何相关洞察力，也没有精力去钻研那些东西。我们光是把精力投入到UI设计上就已经手忙脚乱了。（00:25:22）：这也是我反复强调的观点之一，当人们开始推测通用人工智能可以取代团队成员，哦，设计师不需要工程师，产品经理不需要设计师，每个人都觉得可以把工程部门踢出局时，我会说：别这样。我们都需要彼此，因为我们需要不同的思维模式。其中一种思维模式会完全占据一个人的头脑。我不认为一个人能同时兼具多种思维模式。不是说我的产品经理同事不能为设计出谋划策，而是我需要你专注于自己的位置。就像棒球比赛中，二垒手——

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Like in baseball, the second baseman doesn't cover first. That's not how it works. Everybody's got to spread the field and play their position so we can take care of the whole thing and respect that together we're going to come up with something better than any one of us would've come up with alone and embrace the creative tension, welcome it. We still have to all go out to lunch and love each other and have fun together and keep in mind that we're having fun together, but I like the rub. That's where all the magic happens.
turns.zh: 就像棒球比赛中二垒手不会去守一垒一样。事情不是这样运作的。每个人都需要分散防守位置，各自发挥专长，这样我们才能统筹全局，并坚信共同努力的成果会超越任何个人的智慧，欣然接受这种创造性张力，欣然接纳它。我们还是得一起共进午餐，互相关爱，享受团队时光，但我喜欢这种碰撞——所有灵感都在这种摩擦中迸发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was a very illuminating clarification. Something else that I heard you believe that I haven't heard before is that design share report to engineering.
turns.zh: 这番解释真是令人茅塞顿开。另外，我还听说你认为设计部门要向工程团队汇报工作，这点我之前从未听过。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: So I'll say that every company culture is different and different organizations work in different ways. In my experience, I think that design is most successful at impacting what ships at the end if design is considered phase zero of the engineering process, rather than a by product or a part of the product process. What I've seen happen over and over in my experience, a ThoughtSpot, Pinterest, other places when you're working directly with product, it's easy to leave engineering out of the loop and product and design can go cook up stuff that doesn't quite make sense technically or is really hard to implement or is just a bridge too far. And I think that engineering doesn't feel like they're a part of it, so you bring them at the end and they haven't really been brought along so they don't quite understand how to extrapolate from the specs you make into what should really ship. (00:27:25): Maybe they don't bring the same level of enthusiasm to it, because they haven't been brought along. So I think there's something about having the design and engineering team very tightly connected and kind of living together. And it's not that you have to do that structurally from an organization point of view, but it's hard-pressed if you don't. I also think you can just account for timelines and costs and things better when design's part of engineering. And many of my design friends will push back on this and they'll say design should be its own thing and it should be an independent group and we should have three co-equal branches of government, and that's a solid argument as well, and there's some places where that works beautifully. My experiences at design rarely has a budget or an army, and so it's very hard for them to really hold their own in that sort of a setting. (00:28:09): Also, although you'll see people argue with me on LinkedIn about how design needs to be measured and we need to have metrics and be held accountable for a number, I don't really believe that in my heart. I've just never seen a number that you could apply to design that we could reliably affect. So I think it's very hard to hold design as an organization accountable for a particular outcome the way that most of the other C-level roles are held accountable. Sales has a number, engineering has very specific expectations, product has very specific expectations. And although I know this will frustrate some of my friends, I just haven't been able to figure out how that works for design. And again, it can vary from culture to culture. Certainly there's very successful chief design officers and we could go through the list. I just think in many companies it's a stretch, it's just hard.
turns.zh: 所以我想说，每个公司的文化都各不相同，不同组织的运作方式也大相径庭。以我的经验来看，如果设计被视为工程流程的零阶段（而非副产品或产品流程的一部分），那么设计在影响最终产品发布方面往往最为成功。根据我的经验，无论是在ThoughtSpot、Pinterest还是其他公司，当你直接与产品团队合作时，很容易将工程团队排除在外。产品和设计团队可能会炮制出技术上站不住脚、难以实现，或者根本不切实际的方案。工程团队会觉得自己被边缘化，最终被动接受成果，却无法从你制定的规范中推导出真正可落地的方案。（00:27:25）：或许他们缺乏同样的热情，因为没能被充分纳入决策过程。因此，我认为设计与工程团队紧密协作至关重要。当然，从组织层面不必强制推行这种模式，但若不这样做，后果将不堪设想。此外，设计团队参与工程流程还能更好把控时间线和成本。许多设计界同行会反驳说，设计应该独立运作，形成三个平等的权力分支。这固然有道理，在某些案例中也行之有效。但我的经验表明，设计团队在多数公司缺乏预算支持和资源支持，很难在这种环境中独当一面。（00:28:09）：尽管在LinkedIn上总有人跟我争论设计必须量化指标、接受绩效评估，但我内心深处并不认同这种观点。我从未见过能量化的设计指标能真正产生可靠影响。因此，我认为让设计团队像其他高管层那样为特定成果负责实在牵强。销售有业绩指标，工程有明确的技术要求，产品也有明确的需求预期。虽然我知道这会让一些朋友感到失望，但我始终无法找到适用于设计团队的量化标准。当然，这因公司文化而异。确实有非常成功的首席设计官案例，我们可以列举一二。但在多数公司，设计团队要做到这点实在困难重重。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I see work, and I'm curious to get your take is just product, engineering, design have exactly the same goal and the more everyone... And their performance as an employee is tied to the same thing essentially because then everyone is pushing in the same direction versus like, oh, I have my engineering goal, I have my design goal, I have my PM goal, and just creates all kinds of weird incentives.
turns.zh: 我的经验是，产品、工程和设计团队需要有完全一致的目标，这样才能形成合力。每个人的绩效考核也应该围绕同一个目标展开，这样大家才能朝着同一个方向努力，而不是各自为政。比如，工程师只关注工程目标，设计师只专注设计目标，产品经理只执着于产品目标，这样会导致激励机制严重偏离正轨。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, look, I would kind of defer to you on that, honestly. You've talked to a lot more people across a lot more companies, so you have a much broader set of information you're working with. If you add my whole career together, I've worked at maybe half a dozen places, so a fairly limited sample set. And every design team that I've ever been a part of, I've been a part of. So I also kind of have a biased view as to what didn't work for me in those particular organizations. I'll go back to what I said, every company's different, every culture is slightly different. It's not one size fits all. (00:29:45): I point out the idea of design reporting to engineering just because I don't think people consider the possibility often enough. So there's three options, design is its own thing, design is part of product, design is part of engineering. And I think there's a moment when you can back up and make an intelligent choice about the pros and cons for each of those options inside your org. And so I would encourage people to just take a design mentality and put on that designer mindset just for a moment and say, well, what's the thing that we're trying to produce? What's the incentives that we're trying to create? What's the future state that we're trying to get to? And which of these three options, permutations is going to help us get there the best?
turns.zh: 嗯，说实话，我在这方面可能需要听听你的见解。你接触过更多公司和更多高管，所以你的信息视野更广。而我整个职业生涯只在大概六家公司工作过，所以样本数量相当有限。每支设计团队我都参与过，所以我对那些团队失败的经验也难免带有个人偏见。我还是回到之前的观点，每个公司都有独特的文化，每种文化都略有不同，不存在放之四海而皆准的标准。（00:29:45） 我之所以提到设计向工程汇报的可能性，是因为我发现人们对此考虑得不够充分。设计团队有三种可能的定位：独立存在、作为产品团队的一部分、作为工程团队的一部分。我认为在企业内部，应该结合实际情况，理性评估每种方案的利弊。建议大家暂时换位思考，站在设计者的角度思考：我们要创造什么样的产品？我们要设定怎样的激励机制？我们要达成怎样的未来愿景？在这三种可能的组合中，哪一种最能助我们达成目标？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how radical this idea is. I've not heard it. I think designers will be like, " You stop it. Just stop it." So have you operated this way? Have you had design report to engineering in companies you've worked at?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种激进的观点。从未听过这种说法。我觉得设计师们会说："你别说了。赶紧打住吧。" 你亲身实践过这种模式吗？你所在的公司有设计向工程汇报的案例吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Sorry, but that's how it worked at Apple the whole time under Steve. Design always reported to engineering. Now I think it's structured a little bit differently, but design has always been part of engineering at Apple, so I saw it work quite effectively there obviously.
turns.zh: 抱歉，但在乔布斯执掌苹果期间，这种模式一直沿用至今。设计团队始终向工程团队汇报。现在苹果的架构可能有所调整，但设计始终是工程团队的一部分。显然，这种模式在苹果运行得非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting. Okay, so say just to give someone something very tactical to do on their team, say they don't want to go to this extreme and move the design org under engineering, what's something you've seen work that helps achieve similar outcomes with having engineers integrated early in the design process?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。好吧，如果不想走极端，把设计团队归入工程部门，仅从让工程师尽早参与设计流程来讲，你见过哪些有效的实践？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, look, I think you have to find some way that you are able to identify a few people in engineering that I refer to as creative technologists. So these are people that can come into what's ultimately kind of a fairly airy-fairy philosophical discussion about what we could do and what's right from a conceptual model perspective. Ultimately, it's sort of a philosophy issue. And there's not that many PMs or engineers that can sit in that space and be comfortable with the ambiguity of it all. A PM's likely going to come in and they're going to say, okay, well that was a great one hour. What's the next step? And as a designer I'm always like, well, the next step is we're going to have another meeting and we're going to talk again. And the engineers oftentimes when they're starting to hear different ideas, they're already cutting into the code and they're trying to figure out what's hard and what's easy. (00:31:54): And so I think the trick is at the beginning, can you find a small group of people from the different functions that can sit with the ambiguity of the space and talk through a broad range of ideas to identify the direction we want to go into? And then once everybody kind of falls in love with the direction, then you can go into the more tactical mindset of, okay, well, when we can ship it and who can we show it to and how are we going to code it and when's it going to go live and all those sorts of things. But the trick is to try to find a group that can sit, again, in the ambiguous maybe space. I do think it's critical to have everybody together at the beginning so they all feel like they're part of it. And the worst thing is when you bring something fully baked... Well, the worst thing when you bring something fully baked to anybody for their approval. (00:32:36): We could talk about this when you take a final design to an exec and an exec sees it for the first time in a high resolution state, I'll get to that in a second. But when you go to an engineering team says, "Hey, we've been working in the lab for six months and we have this thing that we love it and we just can't wait for you guys to build it, and here it is," I don't know, [inaudible 00:32:54] mention here. They're going to be excited about. They're not order takers. How do you make them part of the process? And every product of consequence that I worked on, there was some moment when we were showing it to some critical person and you could see that they fell in love with it. Sometimes they're literally pointing at the comps on the board, sometime you're in a meeting and they're just like, "God, I just love this." (00:33:14): And for me, that was always the critical moment because I knew that design can't bring you this stuff into the world on its own. We can't raise this baby, we need the village, and we need the village to fall in love with the baby. And so until that happens, you're not really quite sure if this thing's going to take off or not. And so it was always extremely important to me that you had a few key engineers and some product people fall in love with it so they could defend it and embrace it and enhance it and add to it. And you got to bring them along at the very beginning.
turns.zh: 是啊，你看，我觉得你得找到办法，挑出工程团队中那些我称之为"创意技术专家"的人。这些人能参与到那些本质上相当空想的哲学讨论中，探讨我们能做什么、从概念模型角度来看什么是正确的。归根结底，这就是个哲学层面的问题。能坐在这种模糊不清的讨论中感到自在的PM或工程师并不多。当PM进来时，他们会说，好吧，这次会议很棒，下一步是什么？而作为设计师，我总会说，下一步就是再开个会，再讨论讨论。而工程师们往往一开始就听到不同想法时，就已经开始切入代码，试图弄清楚哪些难，哪些容易。（00:31:54）所以我认为关键在于一开始，能否从不同职能部门挑出少数人，能坐下来接受这种模糊不清的讨论，共同探讨各种可能性，然后确定方向。一旦大家都爱上这个方向，再转入更务实的思维模式，比如何时能上线、向谁展示、如何编码等等。但关键在于，要找到能坐下来接受这种模糊空间的团队。我确实认为一开始就让所有人参与很重要，这样他们才能感觉自己是其中的一份子。最糟糕的情况是，当你把一个完全成型的方案拿给别人审批时……嗯，最糟糕的是当你把最终设计拿给高管看，他们第一次看到高分辨率版本时，我等下再说。但当你去找工程团队说，"嘿，我们在实验室里工作了六个月，做出了这个我们超爱的东西，迫不及待想让你们来实现它，现在就交给你们了"，我不知道，[00:32:54的音频缺失]他们会很兴奋。他们可不是被动接受任务的人。如何让他们参与到整个过程中来？在我参与过的每个重要产品项目中，都有那么一个时刻，当我们向某位关键人物展示产品时，能看到他们爱上了它。有时他们会直接指着白板上的设计稿，有时在会议上他们会感叹"天啊，我太喜欢这个了"。（00:33:14）对我来说，这始终是个关键时刻，因为我知道设计本身无法把产品推向世界。我们不能独自抚养这个孩子，我们需要整个团队的支持，需要他们爱上这个产品。只有这样，这件事才真正有机会成功。因此，让几位关键工程师和产品人员爱上这个产品，让他们能为它辩护、拥护它、改进它、添砖加瓦，对我来说始终至关重要，而且必须从一开始就带他们入伙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing there is there's a big part of just buy-in and then there's also just obviously more good ideas early are great.
turns.zh: 我听你说，这里关键点在于获得大家的认可，还有早期有好的想法当然更好。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, sorry. Buy-in doesn't feel quite right to me, because buy-in feels like, oh, I've come to agree with you. And that's different from it's a part of me. When I'm talking to teams, the thing I try to tell them is, I walk into the office every day with the idea that everyone that I work with is fundamentally a maker. Everybody in product design, engineering, we've all chosen these careers. Everybody's super smart, everybody's super ambitious. Everybody could have done a thousand other things, but they're choosing to spend their precious lifetime and creative energy creating software. (00:34:28): And so I believe in my heart that they're all fundamentally makers. And the thing that I know about makers is that they all want to make something they're proud of so they can take it home at the end of the day and show it to their parents and say, "Look at what I made at school with my friends today." That's the fundamental thing, and they're all doing it from their own different points of view and their own different incentives and mindsets, but they all at the end of the day want to make something they're proud of. And so it's not a matter of getting their buy-in, it's a matter of them being a part of it. I don't know, it's a part of their soul in a really deep, meaningful way. And I'm not sure you can graph that onto somebody after the fact. They kind of need to be there at the moment of inception, if you will.
turns.zh: 是啊，不好意思。“Buy-in”这个词对我来说感觉不太合适，因为“Buy-in”给人的感觉是，哦，我同意你的观点。但这和他们本质上就是创作者是两回事。当我和团队交流时，我试图告诉他们的是，我每天走进办公室时都秉持一个理念——和我共事的每一个人本质上都是创造者。产品设计、工程等领域的每个人，都是主动选择了这些职业的人。每个人都极其聪明、充满雄心壮志。他们本可以做其他无数种工作，但却选择用宝贵的生命和创造力来开发软件。（00:34:28）所以我从心底相信，他们都是天生就想创造出令自己骄傲的东西的人。这样一来，在一天结束时，他们就能把成果带回家，向父母展示：“看，我今天和朋友们在学校做的东西。”这才是根本所在。虽然每个人从不同的视角、基于不同的动机和思维模式来实现这一目标，但归根结底，他们都渴望创造出令自己自豪的作品。因此，关键不在于获得他们的认同，而在于让他们深度融入其中。这在某种程度上是他们灵魂深处的东西，我不确定能否在事后将这种情怀强加给别人。他们必须从项目的初始阶段就全身心投入其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's a really beautiful answer. I imagine for a lot of people hearing this, making every feature and product they build a part of their soul feels like a very high bar if they're building some kind of B2B SaaS software. So I guess just thoughts in just how much you should spend, how much time, how many resources, how deep you go on design for all these things you're building. Say you're building some kind of, I don't know, expense management system or HRS thing, just like, what do you recommend people do with, in terms of just how far to go in design as a lever, as a differentiator maybe?
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个非常精彩的回答。我想对于很多听众来说，把他们打造的每个功能和产品都视为灵魂的一部分，这对那些开发B2B SaaS软件的人来说，可能是个很高的标准。所以我想说说你应该投入多少资源、多少时间、多深的精力来设计你正在开发的这些产品。比如说，你正在开发某种费用管理系统或HRS之类的工具，你觉得人们在设计上应该投入多少精力，将其作为一个差异化因素呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, inherent in your question is this assumption that design takes more time. And so I'm going to kind of reject that premise, because I don't think design takes more time. I think design exists. There is going to be a design. It's whether it's going to be a good one or not. And I think there's things that you can do so that you're able to operate it at a quicker pace as design. Again, if you get the... We haven't talked about tenets yet, but we'll get to that in a moment. If you kind of create a shared philosophical understanding of the product and what you're trying to do, you can go really fast because you're not asking the question of what should you do, you're asking the question of, what would this company with what we stand for do for this thing? And that's a much easier question that's much smaller. (00:36:29): So if you look at the companies that have the largest design teams, they're often the companies that have the most ambiguous cultures and the most unclear design vision. When you go to companies that really know what they're doing and they're clear that this is who we are, this is what we stand for, the design teams are super small because they're not sitting there trying to do all these permutations with color and typography and ideas. They're operating in a really narrow vein, because they know who they are. It's very much like individuals. When you're a teenager or a young adult, you can spend a lot of time trying to figure out what to wear because you haven't really sorted it out yet. But by the time you get to be a little bit older, you've kind of got your personal style, and so dressing in the morning gets to be a lot easier. (00:37:09): Like at Pinterest. I was at Pinterest at a point when Pinterest wasn't quite sure who it was. And so when we were going to do an onboarding flow, we had to look at a really broad sweep of things, because we were trying to sort it out. But you had other places that knew what they were about, Apple's the key example there, we weren't trying to figure out what it was about. We were trying to figure out what was the apple way to do this particular thing, and so that moves a lot faster. (00:37:31): And I agree, look, having your soul at every little checkbox sounds like a high bar and in some ways it is. I think you need to be able to back up and look at the product, maybe not at every state, but generally every six months or a year, you need to back up and ask yourself, am I proud of this? Is this something I am happy to be a part of? Do I believe in this? Is it a representative of my best work given the circumstances I was in, which has limitations around time and resources and everything else, is this the best I could do or am I just sort of trying to get through the day I have other goals?
turns.zh:
嗯，你的问题中隐含着一个假设——设计需要耗费更多时间。那么我要反驳这个观点，因为我认为设计并不需要更多时间。设计本身就存在着，无论是否能设计出好的方案。关键在于你能否以更快的速度完成设计工作。再说回设计原则，我们还没讨论过这个概念，但稍后会谈到。如果你能为产品创建一个共同的理念基础，明确团队的目标和方向，那么设计进程就能大大加快。因为你无需纠结于“该做什么”，而是要问“以我们的核心价值观和理念，如何把这件事做好？”这样更明确、更聚焦的问题。  
（00:36:29）：再看拥有最大设计团队的公司，它们往往文化模糊、设计愿景不清晰。而那些真正清楚自身定位、明确核心价值的公司，设计团队规模反而很小，因为他们不需要在颜色、字体和创意方案上做无穷无尽的权衡。他们专注于核心方向，因为他们深知自己的定位。这就像个人成长——青少年时期可能花大量时间纠结穿搭，到了成熟阶段就能轻松驾驭风格。  
（00:37:09）：以Pinterest为例。早期该公司尚未明确自身定位时，我们不得不面面俱到地设计入门流程。但苹果公司就不同，他们早已明确品牌理念，无需反复磨合。  
（00:37:31）：我认同这个观点——让每个小细节都体现你的灵魂确实是高标准，但确实需要付出代价。每隔半年或一年，你需要回顾产品，问自己：我为此感到自豪吗？我乐于参与其中吗？我认可这个设计吗？考虑到时间、资源等现实条件，这是我能做到的最好结果吗？还是说我只是在敷衍了事？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's actually follow the thread of design tenets and principles. This is something I've heard about you, that you're a big fan of design tenets versus design principles. What is the difference? Why is this so important?
turns.zh: 接下来让我们深入探讨设计原则与设计十诫。听说你非常推崇设计十诫而非设计原则，它们有何区别？为何这如此重要？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, so look, there's whole websites dedicated to design principles, and if you go and you read it, you'll see a lot of principles like simple, clear, beautiful, fast, secure. You'll hear these words and all these words are great. I mean, obviously I have nothing against any of these words, but they're not useful as decision-making tools because nobody would ever argue the opposite. Nobody ever sat in a meeting and said, "Oh, forget clear. Let's try to make it as confusing as possible." So the idea of clear, it's nice to have out there as, I don't know, sort of a platitude to move towards, but I just don't think it helps you make decisions. And so tenets are really decision-making tools and it's sort of like... A classic one is paper versus plastic. It's just too complicated to reconsider that every time you're at the grocery store. So you sort of make a rule for yourself and you're just a paper person or a plastic person, you move on from there. (00:39:07): And so it's sort of that at scale. And the story comes from when they were starting to work on Keynotes, apparently the guy who was responsible for originating Keynote went to Steve and said, "How should we think about Keynote?" And Steve said, "I want you to keep three things in mind. One is it should be difficult to make ugly presentations. Two, you should focus on cinematic quality transitions. And three, you should optimize for innovation over PowerPoint compatibility." And if you take that last one in particular, if he hadn't kind of said, we're going to go this way instead of that way, that team would've spent the next 10 years gouging each other's eyes out over whether they should try to go for PowerPoint compatibility or innovation. And so when I was at ThoughtSpot, I realized pretty early on that I wasn't going to be able to have any sort of command and control over everything that was going to happen in the product. (00:39:56): There was too many people involved, too many engineering teams, most of them were in India. I needed to move from a mindset of control to one of choreography. I needed to try to set the culture and set certain design tenets that everyone could internalize and follow and hopefully then make the right decisions in that groove, if you will. And so we had three, I think you can't have more than three or four because you need everybody to memorize them. They can't be consulting a handbook. And so, one of them was documentation is a failure state. In enterprise companies, a lot of times people think, "Oh, we'll just put it in the manual. It'll be part of the training." And I would constantly be coming back and go, "Stop it. Nobody wants to learn our software. Nobody cares. We are just one more browser tab in a world of browser tabs. We are not this user's complete world. They do not want to learn this stuff." (00:40:46): Documentation's a failure state. Maybe we can't always avoid it, but we should do everything we can to simplify things so you can figure it out in the context of the product. That's number one. Number two is every interaction should start simple and the users should have to opt into complexity. So our main competitor at the time was Tableau. Tableau started with complexity. That was their whole value prop is like, "We're a super powerful tool. We can do all sorts of stuff." So when you sit down at Tableau, it feels like you're flying the space shuttle. And if you're a professional data analyst, that's great. That's the kind of tool you wanted. That wasn't what ThoughtSpot was about. We were trying to take data analytics into the hands of what I call mere mortals, also known as business users, people who didn't live in breathe this stuff every day. (00:41:26): So our goal with them was they could sit down and it was an approachable piece of software and they could turn on all the bells and whistles and power if they wanted it, so that was the second one. Start simple, let the users opt into complexity. And the third one was the entire product should look and feel like it came from a single mind. And this was a tenet to try to combat the natural tendency of enterprise companies to really fragment because you have all these different teams working on their incentive to work just on their little piece. And so they think about what's right for them and they don't back up to look at the whole thing. (00:41:55): And so we had this tenet, the whole thing should look and feel like it came from a single mind to just try to remind people, how does this fit into the whole system? And sometimes we need to go along and do things that work for the product that don't necessarily work quite the way we might want them to for our feature. And so those tenets were all... Again, they were all decision-making tools. And when we would have design debates, we could just come back to this, wait, are we actually starting simple and forcing them to opt into complexity or are we doing something else here?
turns.zh:
是啊，你看，现在有专门讲设计原则的网站，如果你去浏览这些内容，你会看到很多原则，比如简洁、清晰、美观、快速、安全。这些词听起来都很棒。我是说，显然我对这些词没有异议，但它们作为决策工具并不实用，因为没人会反对这些原则。没人会在会议上说：“哦，忘掉‘清晰’吧，让我们尽量设计得复杂难懂。”所以“清晰”这种原则固然好，但它并不能真正帮助你做决策。真正的决策工具应该是一些基本准则，比如“纸质材料还是塑料制品”这样的选择。每次去超市时重新考虑这个问题实在太麻烦了，所以你只需给自己定个规则，要么坚持纸质，要么坚持塑料，然后就此打住。（00:39:07）这就是大规模决策的思路。这故事源自于他们开始开发Keynote的时候。显然，负责开发Keynote的那个人，去找史蒂夫问：“我们该如何考虑Keynote这个产品？”史蒂夫回答：“你要记住三点：第一，难做出一份难看的演示文稿；第二，专注于电影级别的过渡效果；第三，以创新为核心，优先考虑创新而非兼容PowerPoint。”特别是最后一点，如果史蒂夫没有明确方向，团队可能会在是否兼容PowerPoint还是专注创新上纠结十年。后来我在ThoughtSpot工作时，很快意识到我无法全面掌控产品开发的方方面面。

（00:39:56）团队成员太多，工程团队太多，且大部分在印度。我需要从控制型思维转向协调型思维。我得营造一种文化，设定一些设计准则，让每个人都能内化并遵循，这样他们就能顺势做出正确决策。比如我们设定的三个原则——你不可能超过三四个，因为大家得记住它们，不能去查手册。其中一条是“文档是失败状态”。在企业中，很多人觉得“我们把它写进手册，纳入培训就行了”。我总要反复强调：“别这样！没人想学习我们的软件！没人在乎！我们只是浏览器标签页里的又一个选项！我们不是用户的整个世界！他们不想学习这些复杂的东西！”

（00:40:46）文档是失败状态。或许我们无法完全避免，但必须尽可能简化，让用户能在产品上下文中自行理解。这是首要原则。第二条：每次交互都要从简单开始，让用户自愿选择复杂功能。比如我们当时的主要竞争对手Tableau，它从一开始就设计得很复杂。他们的卖点是“我们是超强工具，能做各种操作”。但使用Tableau就像在操作航天飞机。对专业数据分析师来说固然好，但这不是ThoughtSpot的定位。我们想把数据分析带入普通人的手中。
就我所说的普通用户而言，也就是那些非专业人士，他们并非每天都与这些专业术语打交道。（00:41:26）：所以我们的目标是让他们一坐下就能轻松上手这款软件，如果他们愿意，还能开启所有高级功能。这就是我们的第二个原则——从简入手，让用户自主选择复杂度。第三个原则是，整个产品在外观和体验上要保持统一。这是我们努力克服企业公司天然倾向的法宝——由于不同团队各自为战，往往只专注于自己的小模块，导致产品功能割裂。（00:41:55）：因此我们秉持这样的原则：整个产品在外观和体验上要保持统一，时刻提醒用户——这如何融入整个系统？有时我们需要做出让产品更易用但不完全符合我们个人偏好的设计决策。这些原则都是……再说一次，它们都是决策工具。在设计辩论时，我们可以回归这些原则，审视自己是否真正在从简入手，是否让用户自主选择复杂度？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's kind of this implication in this discussion about tenets is that you need to be very opinionated. There's a clear here's what's in and here's what's out. Is there anything more along those lines and are there other tenet examples you could share to give people some inspiration as they think about their potential tenets?
turns.zh: 关于信条的讨论中隐含着一种观点，即你需要有很强的主见。就是那种"这是我们认同的，这是我们反对的"的清晰界限。还有没有更多类似的观点？或者你能否分享一些其他信条示例，为那些正在思考自身潜在信条的人提供灵感？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: It's very context specific, so it's a little bit like what are your tenets for parenting? It's a very specific personal type thing that's germane to your particular context. So I'm not sure if I have a lot of other examples, and I haven't heard this used by a lot of other companies, so I haven't been able to add a bunch of stuff. We tried to come out with tenets for individual features and we had trouble with that. It felt like they operated at sort of the design strategy level. And I just think that varies dramatically from company to company. What I would look for is if you're a design leader or a product leader, try to pay attention to what are the debates that we keep having over and over where people kind of seem to be digging in and things sort of seem to be bifurcating into two camps. (00:43:23): And then is there something we can do where we just have that debate once and for all, we decide as an organization, we're going left instead of right, and you're absolutely correct. You have to be opinionated, but that's how you're going to win. There's no unopinionated software that's been successful. You have to have a point of view. The question is, what's it going to be? So I'd say practically just try to look for places where it seems the team's having the same debate over and over and have it once, get it done, and put it behind you.
turns.zh: 这非常依赖具体语境，所以有点像"你养育孩子的信条是什么？"这类问题。它是针对特定情境的非常个人化的事情。所以我不确定自己是否有很多其他例子，而且我也没听过其他公司用过这个词，所以没法补充太多内容。我们曾尝试为各个功能制定信条，但遇到了困难。感觉它们更多地属于设计策略层面。我认为这在不同公司间差异巨大。我建议，如果你是一位设计负责人或产品负责人，可以留意那些我们反复争论不休、人们似乎各执己见、最终分成两派的议题。（00:43:23）然后，有没有办法能一劳永逸地解决这些争论？比如作为一个组织，我们决定向左发展而非向右发展，你说得完全正确。你必须有主见，但这正是取胜之道。没有成功的软件是没有主见的。你必须有自己的观点。问题是，这个观点会是什么？所以我建议，实际上，要寻找团队反复争论的议题，一次性解决问题，了结此事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And make it a tenet. And why is the word tenet versus principle so important?
turns.zh: 为什么“信条”（tenet）比“原则”（principle）更重要？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: I don't know. I settled on tenet. I'd have to go look up the definition. I was trying to differentiate it from principles because I think principles are just... I describe principles as sort of Applehood & Motherpie. Again, they're just not something people are going to argue over. And so I didn't think it was wise to try to co-op that word and change how people think about it so much as I might be more successful just coming up with a different word altogether.
