turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, look, the example I use mostly is if you go to an airport and you look around, you'll see a lot of people using their phone to navigate that system. They're trying to figure out where their gate is, what time their flight's on, whether or not... Can they pull up their boarding pass, et cetera. And just watch people, watch their faces, watch the level of confusion and frustration. Some of them are tech superheroes like you and me and most of your listeners, but a lot of them are just mere mortals and they're not living and breathing this stuff all the time. And a lot of times they're super frustrated and then take that and scale it out to their entire day. And almost everyone living in a modern economy now is going to have hundreds of interactions with the phone or with a computer. And a lot of those interactions are going to be consequential. (00:46:27): Unfortunately, a lot of those interactions are not going to be great. They're going to be confusing and frustrating. When I'm speaking to live audiences, I often ask people, okay, please raise your hand if you've had a frustrating or confusing experience with software in the last month? And obviously every hand goes up. Okay, how about so far this week? Most all hands stay up. I'm like, okay, how about so far today? And most of the hands stay up, and it's often that I speak in the morning, I'm like, okay, everybody's had a frustrating experience with software and it's 10 o'clock in the morning. That's a problem, people, because each one of those interactions, it takes a little bit of energy away from you and it ramps your frustration just a little bit. And the bummer about software, both for the audience and for the creators is that it's an anonymous medium. (00:47:10): Nobody gets to see who's making these things. You and I together, we might be able to name six designers that have worked on products we care about. And the only reason we could do that is because a designer and I know a bunch of them. By yourself, I'd be surprised if you could name more than a handful. And again, we work in tech. So if you think about the billions of people out there that don't work in tech, to them, these products are just these crazy faceless things created by a bunch of people who knows where, and these products are causing them untold amounts of frustration and confusion, and it just takes away from their life quality. And I think we have an obligation as product people to put that emotional energy back into people's lives. They don't want to try to figure out how to navigate our login screens or go through our onboarding process, they just want to get home and spend time with their families and pet their dogs and have a nice dinner. (00:48:02): I just think every time we make a demand on the audience, that's a failure on our part. And so I do think it comes... I cast it in a moral way, and I talk about it that way because I don't think many people working in the industry understand the scale of what they're doing, again, because it's an anonymous field. We never see anybody on the other side of the glass. (00:48:22): But I think with this podcast, it'll go out to, I don't know, hundreds of thousands of people. If you and I saw all the people that will potentially listen to this in one place, we would think to ourselves, oh my goodness, that's like a lot of people. And we might think of it differently. We might behave differently. My team at Apple, but also my friends that are working at Facebook or Google or wherever, it's very hard to really understand that they're creating something in Figma on their computer that's going to be interacted with by billions of people, thousands and thousands of times. If you lose sight of that I think just, I don't know, you get sloppy and disrespectful is the wrong word, but I think you just lose sight of how much impact you're having on other people.
turns.zh:
嗯，听着，我常举的例子是，当你去机场时，环顾四周，你会看到很多人用手机导航。他们试图找出登机口在哪儿，航班起飞时间是什么时候，能否调出登机牌等等。只要观察人们的神情，看到他们脸上的困惑和挫败感，就能明白这一点。有些人像你我一样是技术达人，但大多数人只是普通人，他们并非时刻沉浸在这些技术中。很多时候，他们会感到极度沮丧，这种情绪甚至会影响到他们的一整天生活。如今，几乎每个生活在现代经济中的人都会与手机或电脑产生数百次交互，而其中许多互动都至关重要。（00:46:27）不幸的是，其中许多互动体验并不理想。它们令人困惑又令人沮丧。当我在现场演讲时，我常问听众：过去一个月里，你们有过令人沮丧或困惑的软件使用体验吗？显然所有人都举手。那这周呢？大多数人依然举手。再问：今天呢？大多数人依然举手。尤其是早上演讲时，大家会发现早上10点就有一半听众举手。这是个问题，朋友们，因为每次这样的互动都会消耗你的精力，增加你的挫败感。对软件来说，无论是对观众还是开发者来说，最大的问题在于它是一个匿名媒介。（00:47:10）没人能看到谁在开发这些产品。就你我而言，或许能说出六位参与过我们关心的产品设计的开发者。而这仅仅是因为我们与其中一些开发者相熟。如果你独自列出名单，可能连几个都列不出来。再说了，我们毕竟在科技行业工作。所以如果你想想那些数十亿不从事科技工作的人，对他们来说，这些产品就是一堆由神秘开发者创造的神秘怪物，正在给他们带来无尽的挫败和困惑，严重影响他们的生活质量。我认为作为产品设计师，我们有责任将这种情感能量重新注入人们的生活。他们不想费力理解如何导航我们的登录界面或完成注册流程，他们只想回家与家人共度时光、抚摸爱犬、享用美食。（00:48:02）我认为每次我们对用户提出要求时，都是我们的失败。我用道德层面来阐述这个问题，也是因为我觉得科技行业的许多人不理解自己工作的规模，毕竟这是一个匿名领域。我们永远看不到屏幕另一端的真实用户。（00:48:22）但通过这个播客，我们的受众可能达到数十万人。如果你我能在一个地方看到所有潜在听众，我们会惊呼：天哪，这可真是不少人啊。我们或许会因此产生不同的思考，采取不同的行动。无论是苹果的团队，还是我在Facebook、谷歌等公司的朋友，都很难真正理解自己正在创造的东西。
他们电脑上的Figma工具，将被数十亿人使用，次数达数万亿次。如果你忽视了这一点，我觉得你就会变得粗心大意、不够尊重用户——虽然“不尊重”这个词可能不太准确，但总之你会忽视自己的设计对他人产生的深远影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's really inspiring. That makes me want to build products and make them awesome. There's so much power to that. What this makes me think about a little bit is kind of random, but when I see someone click and watch one of my podcast videos on YouTube, I'm like, wow, that's one person that's going to spend their time watching this thing. Wow, I really want to make... It gives me more motivation to make these even better and better.
turns.zh: 哇，这真的很鼓舞人心。它让我想去开发产品，并把它们做得尽可能出色。这其中的力量太强大了。说到这，我突然想到一个有点跑题的想法——当我在YouTube上看到有人点击并观看我的播客视频时，我会想，哇，这个人愿意花时间来观看我的内容。哇，我真想把它做得更好、更棒。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, look, I think you have to find ways to go... You have to find where you go out of your way to see people using software in real time. I've worked on products that have been used by billions of people. I have friends who have touched billions of people. None of us ever get to see anybody use this stuff in the wild, in their natural state. Maybe we see them in a lab or something like that, but I've never seen anybody just randomly using even Pinterest. But there's ways that you can go and as a creator, as a maker, you can go and watch people using software in the wild. So just go observe people going through self-checkout at Target, which is the best self-checkout I've ever seen. Go watch that, then go watch it at some other grocery store where it's not as great and really notice what happens with people. (00:50:11): Much to my kids' frustration when their friends are over, I often grab their friend's phone and just sort of flip through it to try to understand how people are organizing their home screens and which apps they use. And maybe there's something in there that I haven't seen, I'll ask them what that is and ask them to give me a tour of it. I think we're living in a time where people don't do so many usability studies, so a lot of folks get pretty far into their careers without ever having watched mere mortals actually use software. Instead, we're relying on metrics and stuff, which I sort of joked that relying on metrics to understand what's happening at the user level is like looking at raw data from a radio telescope instead of just going out inside and looking at the night sky. You got to find a way to watch the audience. (00:50:54): Filmmakers can go to a theater, they can watch people, understand stuff. Comedians can go to a comedy club, they can start to develop an intuition about why people laugh. None of us have an obvious way to go watch people use software, so we don't really understand how humans process what's happening on the screen. And you have to just find ways to do that. And fortunately, software is everywhere. It's not just desktop or mobile software. I mean, there's ATM machines, there's ticketing kiosks, there's point of sale systems everywhere. I mean, go watch somebody over 70 fumble with a chip card insert or watch somebody try to figure out Apple Pay. And these are pretty seamless experiences and still there's cognitive friction in all this stuff. Just go rent a car and notice how long it takes you to figure out what the heck is going on with the dashboard. There's lots of opportunities to try to develop that intuition of how people navigate the human computer interaction, and we need to find ways to do that.
turns.zh: 是啊，你看，我觉得你得想办法去……你得找到机会去观察人们在现实中使用软件的情景。我参与过数十亿人使用过的产品，我的朋友的产品也影响了数十亿人。但我们从未真正看到人们在自然环境中使用这些产品。或许我们在实验室里见过，但我甚至从未随机看到有人使用Pinterest。不过作为创作者和开发者，你可以去观察人们在现实中使用软件的过程。比如去塔吉特超市观察自助结账流程——那是我见过最棒的自助结账系统。再去其他超市看看效果差很多的系统，仔细观察人们的操作。（00:50:11）：每次朋友带孩子来家里玩时，孩子们都烦透了，因为我总会拿起他们的手机，随便翻看一下，看看他们如何组织主屏幕，使用哪些应用。说不定里面有我没见过的功能，我会问他们那是什么，让他们给我演示一下。我觉得我们生活在一个不常做用户研究的时代，很多人在职业生涯中从未真正观察过普通用户使用软件的情况。相反，我们依赖各种指标数据。我曾打趣说，仅凭指标去理解用户行为，就好比用射电望远镜观察原始数据，却不亲自去观察夜空。你得找到观察用户的办法。（00:50:54）：电影制作人可以去电影院观察观众，喜剧演员可以去喜剧俱乐部，逐渐培养对观众笑点的心领神会。但我们没有明显的机会去观察软件使用情况，因此无法真正理解用户如何处理屏幕上的信息。你得想办法做到这一点。幸运的是，软件无处不在。它不只是桌面或移动应用。ATM机、售票亭、销售点系统到处都是。去租辆车，你会发现自己花了很长时间才搞清楚仪表盘上的各种操作。这里有无数机会去培养对用户与计算机交互的直觉感知，我们需要找到实现这一目标的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: An important element of what you're describing here, which I think maybe people miss, is that you're talking about just any software, not your own product, in order to start building your sense of taste and gut feeling for what-
turns.zh: 你所描述的这一点很重要，我觉得人们可能忽略了，那就是你谈论的任何软件，不只是你自己的产品，这样才能开始培养你对用户需求的敏感度和直觉——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Building your sense of taste and gut feeling for what works and doesn't work. And I had a guest on recently, Guillermo Rauch from Vercel, founder of Vercel, and he had a really great phrase of something they do at their company. They have this kind of mission of exposure hours. Increase your exposure hours to people using our product. And then you can extrapolate that to any product.
turns.zh: 培养你的品味感和直觉判断力，分辨哪些方法有效，哪些无效。最近我邀请了Vercel公司的创始人吉列尔莫·劳奇（Guillermo Rauch）做客节目，他提到了他们公司的一个很棒的理念——“曝光小时”。这个理念的核心是增加用户使用产品的曝光时间。然后你可以将其推广到任何产品上。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, well there's using your product, but I always think when you're watching somebody use your product, you come into it with a psychological bias that makes it hard for you to really see what's going on. So there's something about just understanding the audience and how they process information on a screen, not your product. (00:52:40): At one point when I was redesigning a checkout system, we did what I called a reality check, which was we held a traditional usability style exercise in a lab and all that sort of stuff, but we had the subjects come through and go through checkout in other products. So we watched them go through eBay and Williams-Sonoma and Amazon or something like that. And we learned a ton about checkout, about what was important to them, how it turns out ship quote is almost as important as price. Things that if we had been watching them use our own product, I'm not sure we would've picked up on, because we would've been sitting there yelling at them to click on the button. Or we would've had a bias and wanting to see the positive things. Whereas, if you just watch people that are using adjacent products could be super useful. (00:53:22): And again, we work in a medium, software is a medium, and we need to understand our medium in the same way. Again, musicians go to concerts, filmmakers go to movies, comedians go to comic clubs. When do people like you and I go watch people just use software? Where do we develop that intuition? And unfortunately I think you have to go out of your way to do it.
turns.zh: 是的，用户使用产品固然重要，但我总觉得，当你观察别人使用你的产品时，会带有心理偏见，导致你难以真正看清实际情况。所以，了解目标用户群体以及他们如何在屏幕上处理信息（而非你的产品），这一点至关重要。（00:52:40）：有一次我在重新设计结账系统时，我们做了一项所谓的“现实校验”。具体做法是，我们在实验室里开展传统的可用性测试，但同时让受试者在其他平台（如eBay、Williams-Sonoma和亚马逊）上完成结账流程。通过观察他们的操作，我们深刻认识到结账流程对用户的重要性——其中报价功能的体验几乎与价格同等重要。若只是观察用户使用我们的产品，我不确定能否发现这些问题，因为我们可能只会坐在那里催促他们点击按钮，或者带着偏见只关注积极反馈。而观察使用相似产品的用户则会带来极大启发。（00:53:22）：同样，我们身处一个媒介——软件就是一个媒介，我们需要以同样的方式理解这个媒介。音乐家会去听音乐会，电影制作人会去看电影，喜剧演员会去喜剧俱乐部。但像你我这样的人，又在哪里观察用户使用软件呢？我们该如何培养这种直觉？遗憾的是，这需要我们特意去培养。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk about more about this idea that software is a medium. This is something that came up a bunch also in conversations with folks that have worked with you, that this is something that you believe.
turns.zh: 再谈谈软件即媒介这个观点。这也是与合作过的许多人交流时频繁提及的观点，显然这是你深信不疑的。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, you're so good with the research, Lenny. Yeah, look, so I left Pinterest in 2016, sorry, 2016. And I didn't have anything lined up so I had some time to myself and I was driving up and down the peninsula here in Silicon Valley meeting with other design leaders and just sort of commiserating with people. And you may remember there was a very consequential presidential election in the United States in 2016 and there was some impression that social media had had a significant impact on that election. (00:54:22): So I was kind of driving around Silicon Valley and I was just sort of wondering what the heck happened. I moved here in 1990 when the hippie ethos that was really at the core of Silicon Valley, and the hippie ethos was still very visible, it was very much a part of what was interesting to me about the valley when I moved here. But 2016 is a long time later and that hippie ethos had gotten pretty quiet. (00:54:45): And so I was listening to a podcast about the history of Silicon Valley by a Stanford group. The podcast was called Raw Data, and it was season two. And it starts off with an episode called A Monument to a Dead Child, which is about Stanford University, and it ends with Zuckerberg's testimony in front of Congress. And in the middle of that, they start talking about the counterculture revolution in the late 1960s in San Francisco and elsewhere. And they quote this book by a guy named Fred Turner, I think it is, the book's called From Counterculture to Cyberculture. And he has this quote that is, "you have to ask why it is personal computing got started in Northern California in the late 1960s when at the time every major tech company in the country was on the East Coast. And the answer is because there was a very small group of people in and around Stanford University that saw software as a new form of media on par with movies, music and books." (00:55:41): And when I heard that, all of a sudden I went, wait a second, boom. That is why I do this. I am fundamentally a maker. In high school I was a photographer, in college I was going to be a filmmaker, after college I went to music school. After music school I started a graphic design studio. I am a maker. And I realized looking back, I was just hunting for my medium. And it took me until I was 27 to find software as my medium. It's like, oh, I'm a maker that designs software. (00:56:05): And then when I heard that software as a medium, that whole concept of what I'd been doing with my life and who I was about, it just sort of all came together really quickly. And I realized, oh, I am into software because software makes me feel a certain way when it's working well. And what I find so troubling now is that a lot of time it's not working that way. (00:56:27): And I remember the first time I saw a computer, probably a lot of people on listening to the show can remember maybe the first time they saw a desktop computer, probably the first time they saw a pension zoom on a phone. You remember all that stuff. It was just freaking magic man. It was the future. It was so cool, and it just felt like the most amazing aurora borealis, or sunrise, or whatever. There was a sense of awe and wonder that filled me and probably a lot of listeners, that's probably the thing that motivated you to be in the field. (00:56:58): And so I realized software is a medium because there's an emotional component to it. Like a hammer and saw, they're not really pulling out an emotion for me. Maybe there's some, if you're a carpenter, but I don't naturally have an emotion with kitchen tools or things that I think even more sophisticated tools like calculators and pulleys, I still don't have an emotional response to them. But every piece of software I have an emotional response to. I either feel confused or empowered. I feel like my world's gotten bigger or my world's gotten smaller. They all have an emotional component. And I think once you realize and accept that, then you can say, oh, there is an emotional component to what we're doing with this product. I could just leave that to chance, which is what most people do, or I could try to be conscious of it and we could try to bring that into our conception of what the product's about and try to be purposeful in the emotion we're trying to elicit from the user. And I think that's where design and particularly visual design can have a huge impact. (00:57:58): So again, in many conversations that I'd have in design reviews, some executive would go, "I don't know, ultimately this just kind of comes down to a matter of opinion." And I was always like, "no, it does not. Whether we choose blue or red is going to elicit a certain emotional response from the user. What is it we want them to feel? And then let's make sure that we design something visually that evokes that emotion." (00:58:21): So again, I think once you really get your head around the fact that there are people on the other side of the glass, real live human beings having emotional moments with the thing that you're putting in their hand and that they're focusing their attention on. You are in those moments. And are you going to own it and show up and be the person you want to be in those moments or not? (00:58:44): A few months ago, I guess a little longer ago, I was talking to the team at Toast who makes the handheld point of sale stuff that they use in restaurants. And the thing I was trying to tell them, is whether or not you see it, tonight, you're going to be at dinner with a few 100 000 people all across the country. And if we take just one example, you're going to be at a very nice diner with a grandmother and her two teenage sons in Ohio, and the check's going to come and the waiter, the waitress is going to hand over the device to that grandmother, because she wants to pick up the bill. And you have the opportunity to either make her look like a superhero, because she knows what she's doing, or to make her look like a fool and one of her teenage grandsons is going to grab the device and do it for her. (00:59:24): You're at the dinner table, what are you going to do for grandma? You going to show up as well as you can, or are you going to just let this whole thing fall apart, because you didn't think hard enough about grandma? And that's true for Toast, that's true for every product any of us are working on all the time.
turns.zh:
是啊，你真擅长做研究，伦尼。是这样的，我在2016年离开了Pinterest，对不起，是2016年。我当时没有任何后续安排，所以有一些属于自己的时间。我开车在硅谷半岛上到处转，拜访其他设计界领袖，和他们聊聊近况。你可能还记得，2016年美国总统大选意义重大，有人认为社交媒体对选举产生了重大影响。（00:54:22）所以我在硅谷开车时一直在想到底发生了什么。我1990年搬到这里时，硅谷核心的嬉皮士文化理念还很明显，那种嬉皮士精神对我来说很有吸引力。但2016年已经过去很久了，这种嬉皮士精神已经变得很淡薄了。（00:54:45）当时我听了斯坦福大学的一个播客，叫《原始数据》（Raw Data），第二季。第一集讲斯坦福大学的纪念碑，结尾是扎克伯格在国会的听证会。中间他们讨论了1960年代末旧金山等地的反文化革命，还引用了弗雷德·特纳（Fred Turner）的《从反文化到网络文化》一书。书中提到：“你必须问，为什么个人计算在1960年代末的北加州兴起，而当时全美所有主要科技公司都在东海岸？答案是，因为斯坦福大学及其周边有一小群人，他们将软件视为与电影、音乐和书籍并列的新型媒体形式。”（00:55:41）听到这话时，我突然意识到，等等，太对了。这就是我做这行的原因。我本质上是个创造者，高中时我是摄影师，大学想成为电影制作人，毕业后去音乐学校，之后创办了平面设计工作室。我是个创造者。回头看，我一直在寻找属于自己的创作媒介。直到27岁才找到软件这个媒介。就像，哦，我是个创造软件的人。（00:56:05）当听到软件是创作媒介时，我突然意识到，这就是我毕生所追求的，这就是我是谁。然后当听到软件作为媒介的概念时，一切突然串联起来。我意识到，哦，我热爱软件是因为它运行顺畅时给人的感觉很棒。而现在最让我困扰的是，它很多时候都运行不畅。（00:56:27）我记得第一次看到电脑，听众中可能很多人也记得第一次看到台式电脑，或者第一次在手机上看到缩放功能。你们都记得那些东西。简直太神奇了。那就是未来。太酷了，就像最惊艳的北极光、日出之类的。那种敬畏和惊叹感充斥着我，可能也充斥着很多听众，这或许就是你们投身这个领域的初衷。（00:56:58）所以我意识到软件是创作媒介，因为它带有情感成分。比如锤子和锯子，并不会让我产生情感波动。如果你是个木匠，可能会有点感觉，但我对厨房工具本质上没有情感共鸣。
有些东西，比如计算器和滑轮这样的复杂工具，我对它们依然没有情感共鸣。但每款软件都能触动我的情感。要么让我感到困惑，要么赋予我力量。要么让我感觉世界变得更广阔，要么让它变得更渺小。它们都蕴含着情感元素。我认为，一旦你意识到并接受这一点，就能说：哦，我们的产品设计中确实存在情感维度。我可以任由其随机发展（多数人都会这么做），也能有意识地去引导它。我们可以将这种情感融入产品理念，刻意激发用户的特定情绪。我认为这正是设计，尤其是视觉设计能产生巨大影响的地方。（00:57:58）：在许多设计评审会议上，总会有高管说："我不知道，最终这不过是个人观点的问题。"而我总会反问："不，这绝非如此。选择蓝色还是红色都会引发用户的特定情感反应。我们想让他们感受到什么？那就确保视觉设计能激发这种情感吧。"（00:58:21）：再说一次，一旦你真正意识到屏幕另一边的人是真实存在的——那些正用着你交到他们手中、全神贯注关注的产物的人——你就置身于这些时刻之中。你会选择正视并全力以赴，成为你想成为的人吗？（00:58:44）：几个月前，更确切地说，是更久之前，我和 Toast 团队交流过。他们生产用于餐厅的便携式销售终端设备。我想告诉他们的是：无论你们是否意识到，今晚，你们将与全美数十万人共进晚餐。仅举一例，你会置身于俄亥俄州一家温馨的餐馆，祖母和她的两个十几岁孙子共进晚餐。结账时，服务员会把设备递给祖母，让她自己操作支付。你要么让她看起来像个超人，因为她熟练掌握操作，要么让她看起来像个傻瓜，让孙子抢走设备替她操作。（00:59:24）：你坐在餐桌旁，会为祖母做些什么？你会全力以赴地表现自己，还是因为没有充分考虑祖母的需求而让整个过程崩盘？这对 Toast 团队如此，对我们每天致力于打造的产品也同样适用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting and fascinating and inspiring. I was going to ask how you use this insight, that software is kind of the most powerful medium media more than even than TV and movies, and you shared it, which I think is really important. So just to kind of double-down on this, is the advice here is think about the emotion you want the user of your software to have as you're starting the design process, not just what do you want them to do, how fast do you want them to get to this flow, it's what's the emotion you want them to have?
turns.zh: 这真是太有趣、太引人入胜、太鼓舞人心了。我本想问问你如何运用这种洞察力——软件某种程度上是最强大的媒介，甚至比电视和电影更强大，而你主动分享了这些见解，我认为这非常重要。所以我要再深挖一下。这里的建议是，在开始设计流程时，先思考你希望软件用户产生什么样的情感，而不只是他们需要做什么、多快能进入流程，而是他们应该拥有怎样的情感体验？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah. I often don't think about what I want them to do. I just think that's sort of a selfish way to think about it. They have something they want to do. I'm trying to help them. I just don't ever approach these things of the user's something for me to exploit and take advantage of and manipulate. I know there's people that do approach it that way, which I think is a little unfortunate. But as a designer, I guess I have my own set of values and my own kind of compass on these things that's pushed me in a certain way of thinking about it. And so I'm kind of constantly asking what's the right thing for the user? (01:00:44): And I believe in my heart that if we prioritize that wonderful things will happen for all the metrics, including the money metrics that matter. I've never seen a product be successful that used metrics as a driver for what they were doing. I've seen a lot of companies be really successfully seeing metrics as a consequence and a way to evaluate the quality of their decisions, and then using those to triangulate and make better decisions moving forward. So they're kind of a very useful feedback mechanism. But I think there's definitely a risk to confusing, doing something because it's a driver versus something as a consequence.
turns.zh: 是啊。我常常不去考虑用户需要做什么。我觉得这是一种自私的思考方式。他们有自己想做的事，我只是想帮助他们。我从不把用户当作我可以利用、操纵的对象。我知道有些人会这样做，我觉得这挺可惜的。但作为设计师，我有自己的价值观和准则，这让我形成了特定的思考方式。所以我总是在问，什么对用户才是正确的选择？（01:00:44）我深信，如果我们把用户放在首位，所有指标，包括重要的商业指标都会水到渠成。我从未见过以指标为导向而成功的产品。倒是见过很多公司以指标为结果，将其作为评估决策质量的依据，再以此为参照优化后续决策。所以指标确实是很有用的反馈机制。但我认为，如果把指标当作驱动因素而非结果，确实存在混淆风险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a few more questions I would ask, but I want to come back to something that I asked earlier, that I think is on the minds of a lot of say founders and product managers listening to this. I'm just like, okay, this all is sounds really great. I would love to make these experiences so great. It's going to take us a lot of time to do this really, really well. You said that it doesn't have to. What's a tactical tip or two that you can suggest to a founder or product manager to help them contain the design process while also achieving these outcomes that you're describing?
turns.zh: 我还有几个问题想问，但我想回归到我之前提的一个问题，我觉得很多听众，比如创业者和产品经理都很关心。我的想法是，好吧，这一切听起来都很棒。我也想打造出卓越的用户体验。但要把这件事做好确实需要大量时间。你说不必如此。能否给创业者或产品经理一些实用建议，帮助他们在控制设计流程的同时，还能实现你所描述的这些成果？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, I think if you can give... Maybe one way to think about it is like a big giant AI prompt. The more context you can give it, the more specificity you can give it, the more this is what I'm about and what we're trying to get to, the more the designer's going to be able to figure out which swim lane they're supposed to be in to produce something. (01:02:10): So I think if you're going into it feeling like the design process is going to take a lot of time, it's because you haven't been clear in your creative brief, so to speak, which often means you're not really clear in your own head. And I think... I have worked with a lot of founders, and we could identify a bunch of big companies, who I think got started that weren't clear in their own head. I don't want to... Yahoo was an amazing company, but if we just look at Yahoo for a second, I worked there, it was never clear to me what the founding vision of Yahoo was. (01:02:39): And I talk a lot about vision statements and we could say the vision statement of Google is organizing all the world's information. That's a great vision. They'll never achieve that. That's something that's always over the horizon. And it's been a very useful organizing principle for their acquisitions and how the company grows. (01:02:55): Amazon to be the Earth's most customer-centric company. Okay, great. That's a vision, they will never get there. It tells you how they're going to expand. Apple doesn't have an explicit vision, but I might describe it as personal computing can have a transformative effect on the lives of individuals. And I think that kind of focuses a lot of what they're trying to do. (01:03:14): Disneyland, still the best vision statement of all time, which is the happiest place on earth. So once you tell an employee this is supposed to be the happiest place on earth, then you're signaling all sorts of things about how they need to pick up the trash and how they need to show up on time and how they need to wear their uniform. You're just signaling a whole bunch of stuff. (01:03:33): So when I talked to founders, a lot of times they just don't have that clarity of what's the vision of the company. And to go back to Yahoo for a second, I never heard of vision. And so I'm not really sure what they were ever about. They kind of stumbled into the directory and then they added a bunch of stuff around the edges, but it never seemed to make a lot of sense. And so I think people operating inside Yahoo, it ended up being inefficient, because they were having to deal with all that ambiguity. (01:03:54): So I think that that can also be a pretty big risk for founders. They end up caught up with a product idea, and they think that the company is the product, the company is not the product. The product is the product and the company's bigger than the product. And you need to have some vision that speaks beyond just this particular thing. (01:04:12): I think Slack, honestly, both Slack and Pinterest I think are examples of products that became companies, but neither one of those places really knew what to do next, because they didn't have a bigger vision of the change they were trying to see in the world. So back to you, you were asking a very pragmatic question. I think you need to work on your prompt before you go to your designers and try to give them as much clarity about what you want to produce as possible. And I think if you leave it open as to the emotional response you want users to have, you're inviting a lot of ambiguity, which is going to invite a lot of inefficiency.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得如果你能提供……或许可以把这看作是一个大型的人工智能提示框。你提供的上下文越多，越具体，就越能让设计师明白他们应该专注于哪个部分，才能产出符合要求的成果。（01:02:10）所以我认为，如果你一开始就觉得设计过程会耗费大量时间，那是因为你没有在创意简报中清晰表达自己的需求，而这往往意味着你自己对项目的定位也不够明确。我接触过很多创业者，我们能举出许多大公司，它们在创立之初就缺乏清晰的愿景。我不想……雅虎曾是一家了不起的公司，但就雅虎而言，我在那里工作时，始终不明白雅虎的创立愿景到底是什么。（01:02:39）我经常谈到愿景声明。比如谷歌的愿景是“组织全球信息”，这是一个伟大的愿景，但他们永远无法实现。这始终是一个遥不可及的目标，却为公司的收购和发展提供了非常有用的指导原则。（01:02:55）亚马逊的愿景是“成为地球上最以客户为中心的公司”。好吧，这确实是一个愿景，但他们永远无法达成。它为公司的扩张指明了方向。苹果没有明确的愿景，但我可以描述为个人计算可以对个人生活产生变革性影响。我认为这正是他们许多行动的核心。（01:03:14）迪士尼乐园，至今仍是最伟大的愿景声明——“地球上最快乐的地方”。当你告诉员工这里应该是最快乐的地方时，就传递了各种信息，比如要捡起垃圾、准时到岗、穿上制服。这些都是明确的指引。（01:03:33）当我与创业者交流时，他们中很多人对公司的愿景缺乏清晰认知。再说回雅虎，我从未听过他们的愿景，所以我不确定他们的核心理念到底是什么。他们偶然开发了目录服务，然后围绕目录服务添加了各种功能，但始终缺乏连贯性。因此，雅虎内部的运作效率低下，因为员工不得不应对各种不确定性。（01:03:54）我认为这对创业者来说也是一个巨大的风险。他们最终会陷入产品思维，认为公司就是产品，但公司绝不是产品。产品是产品，而公司比产品更宏大。你需要有一个超越特定产品的愿景。（01:04:12）说实话，我认为Slack和Pinterest都是产品先于公司的例子，但这两家公司都缺乏对未来变革的清晰规划。所以回到你最初的问题，你提出的是一个非常务实的问题。我认为你需要先完善你的设计需求简报，再去找设计师，尽可能清晰地传达你希望产出的成果。如果你对用户的情感反应留有余地，就等于在制造不确定性，而这将导致低效运作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that answer. And it's so interesting that AI can help us work better together as humans, because when you find that the AI is not achieving the outcome you want as effectively as you want, that's a lesson. This also translates the working with humans, make the prompt more specific, add more context in life, not just when you're talking to AI.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个回答了。有趣的是，AI能帮助我们人类更好地协作，因为当你发现AI没能像你期望的那样高效达成目标时，这本身就是一种经验教训。这也意味着在与人类合作时，要让提示更具体，增添更多生活情境，而不只是与AI对话时的情况。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. That's so interesting. So the advice here is, if you're finding design is taking too long or you want to just level up your success with your design team, give more context, spend more time on the brief, on what you're actually trying to achieve. And make sure there's a clear vision or mission that everyone can row towards.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。这太有意思了。所以这里的建议是，如果你发现设计耗时太久，或者想提升与设计团队的合作成果，那就提供更多背景信息，多花时间在简报上，在你真正想要达成的目标上用心打磨。同时要确保有一个清晰的愿景或使命，让每个人都能朝着同一个方向努力。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah. Look, design is a problem solving methodology. So the more variables you can remove before they go into the process, the more efficient it's going to be. And if you give designers a lot of ambiguity, they're going to spend a lot of time spinning around, and honestly, that's your fault as the client. (01:05:48): As a design leader, I think one of my main challenges is frankly trying to make the PMs better clients, helping them get more specific. It's very common for a design team to get extremely ambiguous asks from a product team. And the problem for designers, they have to take all that ambiguity and they've got to wring it all out. So when they give it to engineering, engineering knows exactly what to code, because computers don't tolerate ambiguity. Engineers need to know what the thing's going to be. And so design gets stuck with a really ambiguous input, but they have to have a highly specific output and then often timeboxed to do that. And it's just not a recipe for success. (01:06:26): So you're much better off either kind of compressing the PRD experience and bringing the designers into that, kind of co-creating with product and design really rapidly. But you need to... You could think of it in some ways as designers are going to draw the storyboards, and if you don't give them a great script, they're going to have a very hard time. And then you can't give the shooting crew ambiguous storyboards or you're just going to waste untold amounts of money on set. (01:06:51): So if you think about those three steps from script to storyboard to production, it's all about getting rid of ambiguity. And so the more ambiguity that can be removed upstream, the faster design's going to go.
turns.zh: 是的。看吧，设计是一种解决问题的方法论。所以在进入流程之前，如果能尽可能减少变量，效率就会更高。如果给设计师太多歧义，他们就会花大量时间纠结不已，说实话，这都是客户的责任。（01:05:48）作为设计负责人，坦白说，我面临的主要挑战之一就是努力让产品经理成为更出色的客户，帮助他们更清晰地表达需求。设计团队经常接到产品团队极其模糊的需求，这对设计师来说是个挑战。他们必须把所有歧义都理清，再交给工程师，而工程师可不会容忍歧义——他们需要确切知道要编写什么代码。设计师被困在极其模糊的输入中，但却要产出高度精确的输出，还往往有严格的时间限制。这根本不是成功之道。（01:06:26）所以更好的做法是，要么压缩PRD体验，让设计师参与其中，与产品和设计团队快速协作。但你需要……可以这么想，设计师要画分镜脚本，如果你不给他们一个优秀的剧本，他们就会举步维艰。同样，你也不能给拍摄团队模糊的分镜脚本，否则只会浪费大量资金。（01:06:51）所以从剧本到分镜脚本再到制作的三个步骤，都在于消除歧义。所以上游能消除的歧义越多，设计进展就会越快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This begs the question then, you don't want to give designers here exactly. Here's the thing we're designing, make it really great and pretty. There's always this balance of just give designers space to think and be creative and explore. Advice there of just how to navigate that.
turns.zh: 但这就引出了一个问题，你不想给设计师一个准确的描述。这里关键在于，设计师需要设计出出色的、美观的产品。但总要在给设计师足够空间思考和发挥创造力、探索之间找到平衡。这里有关于如何处理这种平衡的建议。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, if you go back to my example of the script and storyboard, scripts don't contain pictures, there's still a lot of opportunity to think differently and to come up with original things and to have a lot of creative input in the storyboarding process. So the script is living mostly in words, which is largely how PMs function. (01:07:39): The thing that I will say, to keep in mind for PMs, there's always a tendency on PMs to want to draw something and then try to give a sketch to a designer. And I would caution them against that. Sometimes they have to draw themselves so they can think it out. But if a PM came to me with something that was drawn and kind of fully baked, my response was like, thanks for giving me that. Now I know exactly what we're not going to do. Because as a point of pride, there's no way I'm going to go execute that exact thing. (01:08:09): So you're right, PMs have to give you the space to operate. And I think a lot of what they're trying to achieve could be done in more informal ways, conversationally and whiteboards, things like that. But yet you need to narrow the problem for the designers, they need constraints. They don't need a tiny little box, but they need constraints. Think in terms of, you don't give them an airport tarmac and you don't even give them a football field. You give them something more like a basketball court, a sort of scale at which they can do their design thing.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果你回看我之前提到的剧本和故事板例子，剧本里是没有图片的，但在故事板创作过程中，仍有大量机会去跳出固有思维，创造出独特的创意元素。因此，剧本主要以文字形式呈现，而这正是产品经理的工作方式。（01:07:39）对于产品经理来说，我想提醒大家一点：他们往往倾向于先画出草图，再交给设计师。但我不建议这样做。有时产品经理需要自己动手画图来理清思路。但如果产品经理拿来一个已经成型的设计方案，我通常会说：谢谢你提供的这个方案，但我们肯定不会照搬。因为作为一个原则，我绝不会去执行这样的方案。（01:08:09）所以你说得对，产品经理必须给设计师足够的发挥空间。我认为很多他们试图达成的目标，其实可以通过更非正式的方式实现，比如口头沟通、白板协作等。但设计师需要明确的限制条件。限制不必太死板，但必须有边界。就好比你不会给他们一个机场的停机坪，也不会给他们一个足球场，而是给他们一个篮球场大小的范围，让他们在此框架内发挥设计才能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about basketball later, but not yet. You've shared a lot of counterintuitive lessons on building product, designing, building teams, leadership. Is there another very counterintuitive lesson you've learned about building products, hiring leading teams that goes against common startup wisdom?
turns.zh: 接下来我想聊聊篮球，但现在先不说。你分享了很多关于产品开发、设计、团队建设、领导力的反直觉经验。还有没有其他与常见创业理念相悖的反直觉经验，特别是关于产品开发和组建领导团队方面的？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: The thing I would say is that you should wait as long as possible to draw a picture. I think that pushes against all the gen AI tools that help you create prototypes. And there's obviously a lot of excitement around that. I can just give a prompt and the AI, they're going to crank out of UI for me. (01:09:21): So I don't think I'm using the term right, but I had this idea from art that I call the primal mark, and that's the first mark that you make on the canvas. And once you make that mark on the canvas, everything you do after that is in response to that mark. It sort of sets your baseline. And so for me, I always felt that as soon as we drew a picture that looked even remotely real, everybody gravitated towards that and said, oh, that's the thing. And people were so uncomfortable with ambiguity that they can't really deal with the tension of, well, that might not be the thing. (01:09:53): And so as soon as you draw a picture that looks even slightly realistic, much less something that comes out of one of these gen AI tools, everybody kind of goes, oh, that's the thing. You just keep doubling down on that thing. And what's happened is you've taken the possibilities from this big broad thing down to this tiny little thing from an AI system that's trained on existing solutions and existing ideas and is maybe not even thinking about it the right way, because all you've really given it is your first-order of thinking. (01:10:22): I think there's a way you can stay in these things conceptually and conversationally, where you can get to your second, third, fourth idea. And that's where stuff gets really interesting. And again, I don't think that has to take a lot of time. That can be over the course of a single meeting, you could get to a second, third, fourth idea. You just have to be willing to not jump at the first thing that looks like a possibility. You get that possibility, you go, okay, well that's interesting, let's table that. What else have we got? (01:10:47): There's one story that kind of related that's useful. In one of my previous jobs, I was responsible for the public website. I remember coming across one of the product managers one day and she's like, "Hey, this link on the home page, we have to make it blue." I was like, "Well, we don't use blue links anywhere." And she said, "Yeah, yeah, but we just have to make it blue." I was like, "Well, we're not making it blue." And a couple of days go by and I saw the home page and the link had been made blue, because she had got around me and she'd gone to engineering and just made it blue. (01:11:11): And I saw her in the hallway again. I was like, "What the hell's up with that?" And she goes, "Well, people couldn't see it." And I'm like, "Oh, they couldn't see it, so it wasn't prominent enough, right?" She's like, "Yeah, it wasn't prominent enough." I'm like, "Well, great. There's a 100 different things we could do to make it more prominent, one of which is making it blue, which is the thing that came to you first because you're not a designer, it's naturally... Because it's the most obvious thing, but it actually doesn't fit in with these larger things we're trying to do." (01:11:36): So I've often... I try to encourage the product managers to what's the problem with the thing? And then let us solve it. Don't jump to it and tell us... Don't tell us this is just exactly what we're supposed to do. And again, I do the same thing on the roadmap. You decide the roadmap, tell us what we're supposed to do, I will ask you about it, and I may push back and we may have some back and forth, but that's your responsibility. I'm going to trust that you are trained and you know what you're doing and you're going to make the right call. And I just want you to give me the same level of respect.
turns.zh:
我的观点是，尽可能晚地开始画图。这与所有能帮助你创建原型的人工智能工具背道而驰。人们对此显然非常兴奋。我只需给出一个提示，人工智能就能为我生成用户界面设计。（01:09:21）：所以我觉得我用词不太准确，但我从艺术中获得了一个概念，叫做“原始标记”（primal mark）。这是你在画布上留下的第一个痕迹。一旦你在这块画布上留下了这个痕迹，之后你做的一切都将围绕这个痕迹展开。它设定了你的基准线。所以对我来说，只要我们画出一幅看起来哪怕稍微逼真的图画，所有人都会立刻涌向它，说：“哦，这就是最终的方案。”人们对模糊性如此不适应，无法应对那种“嗯，这可能不是最终方案”的紧张感。

（01:09:53）：所以只要你画出一幅看起来稍微逼真的图画，更别说用人工智能工具生成的图像了，所有人都会立刻说：“哦，这就是最终方案。”你就会不断强化这个方案。结果就是，你把原本广阔的可能性缩小到人工智能系统训练过的、基于现有解决方案和想法的小框架里，而这些方案可能根本没有正确的思考方式，因为你提供给它的只是最初的想法。

（01:10:22）：我认为有一种方法可以在概念和对话层面保持开放，让你能获得第二、第三、第四种想法。这时候事情才真正变得有趣。而且这并不需要花费大量时间。可以在一次会议中就完成，从第一种想法到第二、第三、第四种想法。你只需要不急于抓住第一个看似可行的方案。当你获得这个可能性时，停下来，说“嗯，这挺有趣的，先放一放。”还有什么其他的可能性？

（01:10:47）：有个相关的例子很能说明问题。之前我在一家公司负责公共网站。我记得有一天遇到一个产品经理，她说：“嘿，首页上的这个链接，我们得改成蓝色。”我说：“嗯，我们任何地方都不用蓝色链接。”她说：“是啊，是啊，但我们就是要改成蓝色。”我说：“好吧，那我们就不改蓝色。”过了几天，我看到首页上的链接已经改成蓝色了，因为她绕过了我，直接去找工程团队改了。

（01:11:11）：我又在走廊碰到她。我说：“这到底怎么回事？”她说：“用户看不到它。”我说：“哦，他们看不到，所以不够显眼，对吧？”她说：“是啊，确实不够显眼。”我说：“好吧，那太好了。我们有100种方法让它更显眼，其中一个就是改成蓝色，但这恰恰是你的第一反应，因为你不是设计师，自然会……因为这是最显眼的，但实际上这和我们要做的大方向不符。”

（01:11:36）：所以我经常……我试图鼓励产品经理去问：“这个问题出在哪儿？”然后我们一起解决问题。而不是直接告诉我们：“这就是我们该做的。”同样，我在路线图上也这么做。你制定路线图，告诉我们该做什么，我会质疑它，可能会反驳，然后我们再来回沟通。
好吧，但这是你的责任。我相信你接受过专业培训，清楚自己在做什么，并且会做出正确的决定。我只希望你能给予我同等程度的尊重。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This advice about not drawing quickly and not making that primal mark, which I love that term, is, I'm curious your take on AI prototyping tools these days. Because that's the extreme version of that. Not only are you just creating a sketch, it's like, oh, it's working, here it is. Here's what it looks like. Thoughts on that, do you discourage people from doing that, PMs especially?
turns.zh: 关于不要快速作画、不要画出那种原始标记的建议——我特别喜欢这个说法——我很好奇你对如今AI原型设计工具的看法。这简直是这种理念的极端体现。你不只是画个草图，而是直接把成品展示出来，说"瞧，它已经能运行了，效果是这样的。"对此你怎么看？你是否不鼓励人们这么做，尤其是产品经理们？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, I think it's a production tool. Once you know what you want and you can give it a really robust prompt, then... I haven't played with it a lot myself, because I'm not in an operational role right now, but presumably it's really useful at cranking out that actionable prototype which you can click and experience. (01:12:43): And I've said for a long time that an interactive idea needs to be expressed interactively, so we're not talking with our hands and we can really understand what's going to happen. So when the idea is ready to be expressed, I think those tools are probably fantastic. But ideas start off pretty fragile, and the best ideas start off really fragile. And I think when you push them to develop too quickly and you put them out in the world and expect them to be able to stand up to critique too early, you're just going to squash them. (01:13:10): I often think about them like the little plant in the Pixar movie, Wall-E, you've got to give that little guy a little space, a little time, some water and some nourishment, and you can't really just suddenly put him out in the wind and think he's going to make it. And so I think a lot of... There's a lot of very fragile, interesting, quiet ideas that I think you need to give some space. And when you jump to the expression of them, I think you're putting them at risk. (01:13:33): I'll also say that, everybody, when they look at a prototype, what they're focusing on is the visual and textual expression. And so as soon as you produce something in high resolution the feedback you're going to get is going to be about colors and shapes and these presentation layer things, which are very loosely related to usability and value. It's like focusing on the special effects of a movie that has a really bad story. (01:13:59): And so at ThoughtSpot, we used to use what we call block brain diagrams, which were even simplified versions of wire frames. It was just big chunky blocks of here's how the screen could be and where things might be located. And because it was so low fidelity, people couldn't get into commenting on what it looked like. We had to talk about conceptually what it was. And so we were trying to build up this firm foundation where we could go from the block frames to wire frames to kind of the final expression. (01:14:24): And I think it helped us clarify what we were trying to do conceptually so that by the time we got to the final visual presentation, that stuff was actually really simple. And initially it made the product team really nervous because we would be sitting in these block frames and wire frames for sometimes weeks, and they'd be like, when are we finally going to see the comps? (01:14:42): And then what would happen, is because we had such a robust design system, once we locked down on the block frames, we could send it to an agency and they could do the full high-res comps in a day, because they knew exactly what they were doing. And so the PMs were always like, what the hell happened overnight? You're like, well, it turns out that the high-res stuff, that's not the hard thing. The hard thing is the heavy lifting of thinking, what are we really trying to do? That's the hard part. (01:15:06): And if you do the high-res stuff, you really muddy the waters. And I think you end up spending a lot more time churning, if you didn't... Again, I'm going to go back to the movie metaphor, because I studied film. If you're trying to fix script issues when you're in production or storyboarding, you're going to churn and you're going to waste a lot of effort. So you've got to figure out what you're trying to do before you go draw the high-res stuff. And I think a lot of the gen AI tools, it's this seductive thing of, hey, let's just go, let's go make the comp and see what we think. I don't really know if you're going to get anything great out of that process, maybe.
turns.zh:
嗯，我觉得这是一个生产工具。一旦你清楚自己的需求，并能给出一个非常清晰的提示，那么……我自己没怎么用过它，因为我现在不在运营岗位上，但我想它在快速生成可点击、可体验的原型方面确实很有用。（01:12:43）而且我一直认为，一个交互式创意需要以交互方式呈现，这样我们才能真正理解接下来会发生什么。所以当创意准备好要呈现时，这些工具可能非常棒。但创意一开始往往很脆弱，最好的创意一开始也非常脆弱。我认为如果过早地推动它们发展、将它们推向市场并期望它们能承受批评，那只会把它们压垮。（01:13:10）我常把它们比作皮克斯电影《机器人总动员》里的那株小植物。你得给那小家伙一点空间、一点时间、一些水和养分，不能突然把它暴露在风雨中还指望它能挺得住。所以我觉得很多……有很多非常脆弱、有趣、安静的创意，你需要给它们一些空间。当你急于将它们呈现时，你其实是在把它们置于危险之中。（01:13:33）我还要说，大家看原型时，关注的都是视觉和文字表达。一旦你做出高分辨率的成果，得到的反馈就会是关于颜色、形状和这些表现层的东西，这些和可用性和价值关系不大。这就像关注一部剧情糟糕的电影的特效一样。（01:13:59）在ThoughtSpot，我们过去常用所谓的块状脑图，这甚至是线框图的简化版本。就是用大而粗糙的块状图展示屏幕可能的样子和元素可能的位置。由于低保真度很低，人们不会去评论它看起来如何。我们必须从概念上讨论它是什么。因此，我们努力建立一个坚实的基础，从块状框架到线框图，再到最终的呈现。（01:14:24）我认为这帮助我们在概念上理清了我们要做什么，这样当我们最终进行视觉呈现时，事情就变得非常简单了。最初这让产品团队很紧张，因为我们有时会在块状框架和线框图上坐上好几周，他们会问，什么时候能看到最终的排版图？（01:14:42）然后会发生什么呢？因为我们有非常强大的设计系统，一旦确定了块状框架，我们就可以把它交给代理公司，他们可以在一天内完成高分辨率的排版图，因为他们完全清楚该怎么做。于是产品经理总是问，天哪，一夜之间发生了什么？你会说，嗯，原来高分辨率的东西不是最难的，最难的是进行沉重思考，思考我们到底要做什么？这才是难点。（01:15:06）如果你过早地做高分辨率的东西，就会把事情复杂化。我认为你最终会花更多时间反复修改，如果你不……再说回电影比喻，因为我学过电影。如果你在制作或故事板阶段试图修复剧本问题，你会陷入反复修改，浪费大量精力。所以你得
先得搞清楚自己想做什么，再去画高分辨率的图。我觉得很多生成式AI工具都有种诱人的感觉——嘿，咱们先试试看，先做个对比图，再看看效果如何。但我真不确定通过这种方式能创作出什么特别出色的作品，或许也未必能达到预期效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really interesting counter-narrative because it feels like every team now is just straight to prototypes. I just had the C... She's one of the CPOs at Microsoft. I realize there's many CPOs, and she has this concept of demos before memos and just prompt sets or any PRDs, you should just be prototyping all your ideas. And so it's interesting to hear the perspective of maybe it's actually hurting your ability to come up with a really clever solution versus the obvious solution.
turns.zh: 这真是一个有趣的反叙事，因为现在似乎每个团队都直接进入原型阶段。我刚见了微软的某位首席产品官。她提到了在备忘录之前先做演示，或者直接制作原型文档的理念。她认为你应该把所有想法都先转化为原型。听她谈论这个观点很有意思——相比显而易见的解决方案，这或许反而会阻碍你想出真正巧妙的方案。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah. Look, I think at some point, hopefully people just back up and ask themselves, are we actually producing better product because of this process? And we're going faster, but faster can't be the ultimate goal. You need to be creating something great as well, right? Something that's sustainable and frankly that you're proud of and your users find value in. And if you're just throwing so much spaghetti at the wall, I don't know if having a spaghetti throwing machine that goes faster is... (01:16:35): Look, there's a counter argument that's... You can say, oh, it's like Darwinian evolution, and we're just going to spin through a bunch of random mutations and see what happens. And I used to joke that it's true, that if you take a bunch of hydrogen atoms and give them 14 billion years, you could end up with a tiger, but you don't know you're going to get a tiger and you could get a six headed shrimp instead, and you don't really know when it's going to shift. So I'm not exactly sure Darwinian evolution is the way we create great product, but a lot of companies are making a run at it.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得有些时候，希望人们能退后一步，问问自己：我们真的因为这个流程就能产出更好的产品吗？速度是快了，但速度不应该是终极目标。你还得创造出优质的东西，对吧？要能经得起考验，坦白说还要让你引以为傲，让用户觉得有价值。如果你只是胡乱尝试各种想法，我不确定速度更快的尝试就能带来更好的结果……（01:16:35）：有种反驳观点是……你可以说这就像达尔文进化论，我们就是要尝试一堆随机变异，看看结果如何。我以前开玩笑说，如果把一堆氢原子放在那儿，让它们经历140亿年演化，最终可能出现老虎，但你不知道会出现老虎，也许会是六头虾呢，而且也不知道什么时候会发生转变。所以我不确定达尔文进化论能否成为我们创造优质产品的途径，但很多公司正在尝试这种做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to take us to a recurring segment on the podcast called AI Corner. And in AI Corner, I ask guests to share what's one way that you've learned or figured out to use AI in your job to help you do better work, to help you do faster work?
turns.zh: 接下来我们要进入播客的常规环节——“AI角落”。在这个环节里，我会邀请嘉宾分享他们在工作中利用AI提高效率、提升质量的经验。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Well, my job right now is trying to figure out what my job is. And so the thing I've been using AI for is I've very explicitly been using it as a life coach. And so I had seen a couple of prompts about asking it what a blind spot was or what my strengths and weaknesses were. I'd seen some prompts about that stuff. (01:17:34): And one of them was really fantastic. One of them was, what's an outdated mindset that I'm holding onto that's not still serving me? And it came back with a very polite prompt or very polite response about, well, given your age and your profession, it's not surprising that you're very wedded to the idea of control, but that's not really the world we're living in anymore. And that's not probably going to suit the thing you're trying to do next, which is writing and publishing and speaking and stuff. And although it's statistically derived, it did come back with a really nice phrase, which I view...
turns.zh: 嗯，我现在的工作就是在探索我的工作到底是什么。我目前用AI的场景就是把它当作人生导师。比如，我看到过一些提示，比如询问我的盲点是什么，优势和劣势在哪里。我还看到过一些类似的提示。（01:17:34）：其中有一个特别棒。它问我：“你现在还固守着哪些已经过时的思维模式？”然后给出的回复特别礼貌，说：“考虑到你的年龄和职业，执着于控制权并不奇怪，但这已经不符合当今世界的规则了。这可能不适合你接下来的写作、出版和演讲等工作。” 虽然这是统计得出的结论，但回复的语气很贴切，我觉得……

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Although it's statistically derived, it did come back with a really nice phrase which I've used in your show, which was, try to focus on choreography over control. (01:18:08): And so I thought that was really useful. I asked for some of my blind spots, that was also useful. I use it for a lot of exercise input, that's useful. And the exercise that I've gone through most recently was I realized that it was inferring these things about me from the things that I had asked it to help me with in the past. (01:18:26): So instead, I just switched. I just went to ChatGPT, start a new project and said, I want you to be my life coach. I want you to ask me five questions a day for the next five days. Let's go through those so you can explicitly become better at helping me with this task. (01:18:40): And so we've just gone through that process and it's been really useful for me. It's no substitute for a therapist or a real coach or anything like that. It's not a human being. It doesn't care about me. I'm not saying that you should use it instead of these other options. You need a human being as well. But it's been very good at reflecting back to me things that I think have been floating around in my undermind. (01:19:03): So there's a wonderful book called Hair Brain Tortoise Mind by a gentleman named Guy Claxton. In that, he talks about the undermind. And sometimes you might've heard this as your unconscious or something like that. But I think of your undermind as the part of your brain that's processing information before it gets to language. And then when you go to consciousness, you've turned it into language. (01:19:25): And language isn't the full universe of things you can think, language is what you can think in English. And if you talk to multilingual speakers, they'll tell you that they can think things in other languages than what they can think in English. (01:19:35): So if you only speak English, you're only in one vein of what you could think, but your undermind is operating through all this other stuff. And for the computer nerds out there, you could think about it as a compiled code versus interpreted code. (01:19:46): So your undermind work in a compiled code and it could do a lot of stuff that you can't really do in the interpreted code which moves slower and has different orientations and we call that consciousness. (01:19:56): So I was feeding ChatGPT all this stuff over the last year or so, and there are all these patterns in my undermind that had been going into that I wasn't able to express with conscious language. (01:20:08): And so when I started asking it questions, I think what it was doing was it was statistically reflecting patterns back to me that already existed in my undermind, but because it was putting them into language, my conscious mind could now recognize them and respond to them. (01:20:21): And so again, as a life coach, I found it very useful as a mirror back to things that I was probably already thinking. And it helped me clarify my thoughts. It's not pushing me in new directions that a human might do, but it's still been super useful.
turns.zh: 尽管这是通过统计分析得出的结果，但它确实给出了一个很棒的建议，我在节目中用到了这句话："要专注于编舞而非控制"。（01:18:08）我觉得这非常有用。我还请它指出我的盲点，这也很有帮助。我用它来获取大量锻炼建议，这也很实用。我最近经历的一次锻炼是意识到，它是根据我过去寻求帮助的需求来推断我的性格特征的。（01:18:26）于是我换了一种方式。我直接对ChatGPT说："我需要你成为我的生活教练。接下来五天，每天问我五个问题。让我们一起探索这些问题，帮助我更好地完成这项任务。"（01:18:40）通过这个过程，我收获颇丰。虽然它无法替代心理治疗师或真正的人生导师，但它确实能反馈出我潜意识中未被察觉的想法。（01:19:03）有一本很棒的书叫《毛发脑、乌龟心》，作者是盖伊·克拉克森。在书中，他探讨了潜意识。有时你可能听说过"潜意识"或类似概念。但我认为潜意识是大脑在语言形成前的信息处理阶段。当信息进入意识层面时，我们用语言将其表达出来。语言并非人类思维的全部维度——它只是用英语表达的思维范畴。与多语言者交流时，你会发现他们用其他语言思考的能力远超英语。（01:19:35）所以如果你只会英语，你只能局限于一种思维模式，而潜意识却在处理其他信息。用计算机术语来说，潜意识就像编译代码，而意识则像解释代码——后者速度更慢、方向更明确。（01:19:46）过去一年左右，我不断向ChatGPT输入各种信息，发现潜意识中存在许多未被意识层面表达的模式。（01:20:08）当我开始向它提问时，我认为它其实是在反馈我潜意识中已有的模式。通过语言化呈现，这些模式得以被意识层面识别并做出回应。（01:20:21）作为人生导师，我发现它像一面镜子，反射出我可能已有的想法，帮助我理清思路。虽然它无法像人类那样引导我走向新方向，但依然非常实用。

turns.en: That is extremely cool. That is a really cool use case. I don't know if you've heard the Jerry Colona episode that I did recently. Okay, we'll link to it. He's got four questions that he suggests people ask themselves. (01:20:50): The first is the title of the actual episode, how are you complicit in creating the conditions you say you don't want? And this often leads to a lot of interesting insights about yourself, and there's an important part of it, complicit being like you're not responsible, but you're actually helping achieve a thing.
turns.zh: 太酷了。这真是个超棒的应用案例。我不知道你有没有听过我最近做的那期关于杰瑞·科洛纳的节目。好的，我会附上链接。他提出了四个建议人们自问的问题。（01:20:50）：第一个问题是那期节目的标题——你如何在不知不觉中助长了自己口口声声抗拒的现状？这个问题往往能让人对自己有深刻的认识，其中关键点在于“共谋”这个词——它并非指责任，而是指你实际上在助长某种局面。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: It's a powerful word. Yeah.
turns.zh: 这是个很有力的词。是啊。

turns.en: And then also it's an important element of say you don't want, you say you don't want to be busy, but something you just keep creating busyness for yourself, maybe you do want this. So anyway, we'll link to that episode. There's a lot of good stuff there.
turns.zh: 还有，这也是个重要的要点——比如你说不想忙碌，但却总在给自己制造忙碌感。或许你其实渴望这种状态。总之，我们会附上那期节目的链接，里面有很多精彩内容。

turns.en: Okay, one final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. This is one that I don't think you have any idea I'm going to ask you about. And so I'm curious where this goes. (01:21:32): This is a story that Joff Redfern suggested. I ask you. He told me that you're obsessed with space. You love researching space, telling stories about space. There's a story that you share about this guy named John Hobolt. Does that ring a bell?
turns.zh: 好，在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后再问一个问题。我觉得你肯定猜不到我要问什么。真好奇结果会怎样。（01:21:32）：这是乔夫·雷德费恩提议的一个故事。我问问你。他告诉我你痴迷于太空，热爱研究太空、讲述太空故事。有一个关于约翰·霍博尔特的故事，你听说过吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: So I should clarify, I am a fan of astronomy and space, but I'm a particular fan of the Apollo program because I view the Apollo program and the moon landings as the greatest peacetime accomplishment of mankind ever. (01:22:06): And I think it's an incredible... There's a profound number of leadership lessons and individual lessons to be learned from that program. And I've done multiple talks about this. I could go on for hours.

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: The particular question you're asking is John Hobolt. So, John was, I can't remember exactly where he was at the NASA hierarchy, but he was one of the people that was tasked with figuring out the question of how do you go to the moon? (01:22:34): So just to take yourself back in history a little bit, John Kennedy, president Kennedy goes to Rice University, I believe it's 19 September or May 1962, he gives the famous moon speech, we choose to go to the moon not because it's easy, but because it is hard, that whole thing, which I also have to say, and maybe a link to this in the show notes as well, everyone should go watch that talk. That is the perfect Ted talk. (01:22:54): It clocks in right at 18 minutes. It shows you how to sell a big, giant, bold vision. The specifics that Kennedy gets into the way he sets context at the beginning, the technical problems are going to happen, how much money it's going to cost, the way he puts the passion, why we're going to go to the moon, the whole thing. (01:23:09): It is an incredible talk. It's the only moonshot talk ever because a moonshot has to actually go to the moon. And so it is an incredible talk. So go watch the talk. But he steps off the stage and people at NASA are like, we've only recently put Alan Shepard into space. (01:23:27): And he just went up and went down. That was almost like it was a blue origins type thing that was just up and down. We didn't even do a lap around the earth like the Russians did with Yuri Gagarin. And now we're talking about going to the moon. Nobody knows how to go to the moon. (01:23:40): And there was three different options for going to the moon, one at the time, one was to build a big giant rocket and just go straight to the moon. It's called direct ascend. And the main advocate for that was Warner von Braun, who was the main rocket guy in the world. A little bit of a complicated past. (01:23:53): But nevertheless, Warner von Braun's a big guy. He is, got the president's ear. He's like, let's build a big giant rocket, go to the moon. People are like, yeah, the problem is when you get to the moon, the rocket's still super big. So these guys are going to have to descend a big ladder. That's a problem. So that was one idea. (01:24:07): There was another called Earth Orbit Rendezvous where you spend two spacecraft into Earth and then you link them up in Earth orbit and then one of them goes off to the moon, but you still got to land that thing on the moon. (01:24:18): And then there's a third idea called Lunar Orbit Rendezvous, which is where you build a spacecraft that includes a smaller spacecraft. So you send up two spacecraft together, one of them's smaller, much lighter, and you use that just as the ship that goes down to the moon's surface and back up. (01:24:31): And that spacecraft is truly a spacecraft. It only flies in space, which means the engineering requirements around it are profoundly different because it doesn't have to survive re-entry into the earth. And so as a result, it can be much lighter. (01:24:45): And it turns out that the whole problem of landing on the moon is it's a weight problem. You got to lift all the stuff off the earth, which is incredibly expensive for fuel. You got to land it on. There's just a lot goes on. And so Hubert had come across this paper from a gentleman named Yuri Kondrachev who was living in Ukraine in the 1916, 1918 when he wrote this paper. (01:25:05): And he was the first guy to theorize Lunar Orbit Rendezvous. And I try to take people back to that. You and I can think about going to the moon, but Yuri Kondrachev in 1918 is on the plains of Ukraine looking at the moon, and he's actually thinking about how to really go to the moon. (01:25:23): He's figuring it out. And so he writes this paper, John discovers it years later, and John's trying to sell Lunar Orbit Rendezvous. It's not going over at NASA. And so eventually he decides to go around all the hierarchy and he sends a very famous memo to one of the top guys at NASA. (01:25:39): The memo starts somewhat as a voice in the wilderness and then it goes on. And then there's points in there where he's really emphatic, do we want to go to the moon or not? And then he goes through all the math of how going to the moon is all about weight and this was the only way to do it, and there was no other option, stuff like that. (01:25:54): He just made the case and he risked his whole career. The whole thing could have blown up. He could have been fired for going around the hierarchy and all that sort of stuff, but of course, he's able to champion the idea. (01:26:04): And I think it was another year or so after that famous memo, which you could read online, it's nine pages long or something. After the memo, it was still some time before they adopted Lunar Orbit Rendezvous, but eventually they do. And even with Don brought himself was very complimentary to ALT for pushing that perspective. (01:26:21): So I tell the story, one, because it's just amazing story and it does force you to go back to the moment of like, wait, they didn't actually know how to do it. We only know how to do it now because they've done it. But there's that moment of uncertainty and I think you have to embrace and be amazed at that. (01:26:41): And it also shows you the power of these ideas. A really great idea somehow finds a way to live on somehow it just sits out there and it just waits for its time. And Yuri had brought this idea into the world and it just sat around and then somebody it and dusted it off and was able to push for it and it came through. (01:26:58): Then maybe the third lesson is ideas need champions. They need champions willing to put themselves on the line for them. If you believe in something and you've made your case and you can really make your case, have the courage of your convictions and get behind it and fight as hard as you can for it.
turns.zh:
您提到的具体问题是关于约翰·霍博尔特（John Hobolt）的。所以，约翰在NASA的职位层级我记不太清了，但他是负责研究如何登月问题的人员之一。（01:22:34）首先，让我们回顾一下历史背景。1962年9月19日或5月19日，肯尼迪总统在莱斯大学发表了著名的登月演讲。他说：“我们选择登月，不是因为这容易，而是因为这困难重重。” 我还得说一句，或许可以在节目笔记中附上链接，建议大家都去看看那场演讲。这是TED演讲的典范之作，时长刚好18分钟。它向你展示了如何推销一个宏大而大胆的愿景。肯尼迪在开场时设定背景，提到技术难题、资金投入，再到激发热情、阐释登月意义等，每个环节都处理得非常到位。（01:23:09）这场演讲堪称完美。它是唯一真正实现登月目标的"登月计划"。因此意义非凡。大家一定要去看看这场演讲。但当他走下舞台时，NASA的人却在说："我们最近才把艾伦·谢泼德送上太空啊。"（01:23:27）而他的演讲就像蓝色起源公司的太空飞行演示——直接升空又降落。我们甚至没有像俄罗斯用尤里·加加林完成的那样绕地球一圈。如今却要讨论登月问题。谁知道该怎么做呢？（01:23:40）当时有三种登月方案。第一种是直接升空，使用巨型火箭。这是华纳·冯·布劳恩的主张，他是当时世界顶尖的火箭专家，但其背景略显复杂。（01:23:53）不过冯·布劳恩确实影响力巨大，获得了总统的支持。他主张建造巨型火箭直冲月球。但问题是到达月球后，火箭仍体积过大，所以宇航员得从大梯子上下来。这是个难题。第二种方案是地球轨道交会，即将两艘航天器送入地球轨道后对接，其中一艘再前往月球。第三种是月球轨道交会，即制造包含较小航天器的组合体。两艘航天器共同升空，其中较小的那艘更轻敏捷，用于登月返回。（01:24:31）这种航天器完全专注于太空飞行，工程要求截然不同，因为无需承受重返大气层的压力。因此它可以更轻便。（01:24:45）结果发现登月的核心难题在于重量问题。要把所有装备从地球带上月球，燃料成本极高，还要确保安全着陆。重重挑战接踵而至。赫伯特偶然发现了尤里·康德拉切夫的论文。这位1916至1918年间在乌克兰的科学家，是第一个提出月球轨道交会理论的人。（01:25:05）我们现在回顾历史，但尤里·康德拉切夫才是真正开创登月先河的人。
1918年，康德拉切夫站在乌克兰平原上凝视着月亮，实际上他正在思考如何真正登上月球。（01:25:23）他正在仔细思考这个问题。多年后，约翰发现了这份研究报告，而约翰当时正试图推销“月球轨道会合”计划，但该计划在NASA未获青睐。最终，他决定绕过层层官僚程序，向NASA高层发送了一份极具争议的备忘录。（01:25:39）这份备忘录最初像是孤立的呼声，但随后内容逐渐激烈起来。他反复强调：“我们到底想不想登月？”接着他详尽阐述了登月任务对重量控制的要求，以及除此之外的其他方案皆不可行的论点。

（01:25:54）他冒着职业生涯风险全力捍卫这一构想。若未能成功，他很可能遭到解雇。但最终，他成功说服了上层领导。（01:26:04）在这份九页长的备忘录发布约一年后，NASA才最终采纳了月球轨道会合方案。即便如此，Don仍对ALT推动这一理念的勇气赞赏有加。

（01:26:21）我讲述这个故事，一是因为它太令人惊叹，它迫使我们回想起那个时刻——等等，他们当时根本不知道怎么做。我们之所以现在知道，是因为他们已经成功了。但当时存在着不确定性，我认为我们必须正视并惊叹于这种不确定性。

（01:26:41）它还展示了这些想法的力量。一个伟大的构想总能找到生存之道，静静等待时机。尤里将这个构想带入世界，它被搁置许久，直到有人重新发掘、赋予其生命力并成功推进。

（01:26:58）第三个启示是，想法需要拥护者。他们需要愿意为之冒险的勇士。如果你坚信某个构想，做好充分论证，就要有坚定的信念，挺身而出，为之全力争取。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a great story. I love that you summarize the takeaways too, by the way. So to me, the takeaways and the lessons here is one is coming back to your Pinterest board in the office, say the hard thing. (01:27:28): Two is be patient. It may take a little bit of time for a radical idea, especially to resonate and stick and get adoption. So if you're pitching a big new product idea, don't assume that they'll immediately agree. Also, just this idea of if you really believe in it, do go and champion it. There needs to be someone passionately arguing for this.
turns.zh: 真是个精彩的故事。顺便说一句，我很欣赏你总结要点的做法。在我看来，关键要点之一是回归到办公室的Pinterest板上，勇于说出难事。（01:27:28）第二点是保持耐心。一个激进的想法要想在市场上立足、被广泛接受并获得成功，可能需要一定的时间。所以如果你在推销一个新产品概念时，别指望对方会立刻同意。此外，如果你真的对这个想法深信不疑，就应该积极去倡导它。必须有人充满热情地为之发声。

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, I'll just add to that one thing. I think people need to understand that they're advocating for ideas and not for themselves. And when I talk to a lot of designers that may be true for PMS, I hear a lot of people say that they're reluctant to post on social media or on LinkedIn or something because like, "Well, I don't want to be self-promoting." (01:28:06): And I try to counsel them like, look, it's not about self-promotion. There are ideas that you care about that you want to see succeed in the world. And so get out there as an advocate of the idea. It's not about you, it's about the idea. And don't be afraid to stand behind the idea.
turns.zh: 是的，我再补充一点。我认为人们需要明白，他们倡导的是理念而非个人。当我与许多设计师交流时，特别是关于产品管理系统（PMS）时，常听到有人说不愿在社交媒体或领英上分享内容，理由是“我不想自我推销”。（01:28:06）我会这样劝慰他们：这不是自我推销的问题。有些你深信不疑的理念，值得让世界看到它成功。作为这个理念的倡导者挺身而出吧。这关乎理念而非你个人。别害怕为理念站台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've spread a lot of good ideas in this conversation, Bob. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 鲍勃，我们在这次对话中分享了很多好点子。现在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节，你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: Yeah, let's go.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We added a ding to this. I like that drama you added and there's a whole thing now. Okay, first question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 我们增加了一个环节。我喜欢你加的戏剧性元素，现在整个环节更精彩了。好，第一个问题，哪些书是你最常向别人推荐的？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: So the three books I'm going to recommend, the first one's a beautiful poetic book about typography called The Elements of Typographic Style by Robert Bringhurst. Robert was the poet laureate of Canada. And the first 80 pages will change how you think about typography. (01:28:59): It will open you up to the wonderful world of typography that we all live in. You'll think differently about every sign you look at, about every movie credit you see, and it will give you an insight into the designer mindset. When you understand typography, I think you understand where designers come from and the best designers I know are just total type nerds. So highly recommend Elements of Typographic Style. (01:29:23): Second book, Zen and the Motorcycle Maintenance. Many people may know ultimately a philosophy book, but it's about the concept of quality, which I think is a very important topic. So it talks about quality and the importance of how things integrate into cohesive whole, which I believe is the main challenge facing most software teams. They create something that's highly fragmented instead of a single hole. So, Zen in the Motorcycle Maintenance. (01:29:46): And then the last one is a book called Time in the Art of Living by Robert Gruden. It's just a very interesting collection of impressionistic views of time and how time passes and what time means. So that's very different from the others and it's not something probably gets recommended on your show too often, but I think it'll help people in their lives in a powerful way.
turns.zh:
我要推荐的三本书，第一本是罗伯特·布林赫斯特（Robert Bringhurst）的《排版风格的要素》。这本书讲述了排版的诗意之美。罗伯特曾是加拿大桂冠诗人。前80页将彻底改变你对排版的认知。（01:28:59）它会带你领略我们所处的奇妙排版世界。你会以不同视角看待每一块标识、每一部电影的字幕，这本书还能让你深入了解设计师的思维模式。理解了排版，你就能理解设计师的来源，我认识的最优秀的设计师都是排版狂热分子。强烈推荐《排版风格的要素》。
（01:29:23）第二本是《禅与摩托车维修艺术》。很多人可能只知道这是本哲学著作，但其实它探讨的是质量理念，我认为这是个非常重要的主题。书中谈到质量，以及如何让事物融为一个连贯整体的重要性。我相信这正是多数软件团队面临的主要挑战——他们开发出碎片化的产品而非完整的整体。所以，《禅与摩托车维修艺术》值得一读。
（01:29:46）最后一本是罗伯特·格鲁登（Robert Gruden）的《时间：生活艺术》。这是一本有趣的书，收录了对时间的印象派观点、时间流逝的思考以及时间的意义。与其他书籍截然不同，可能也不常在你的节目中被推荐，但我相信它能给人们的生活带来深远影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think these are all brand new entries in this question. Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我觉得这些都是这个问题的新视角。下一个问题，你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: So I really enjoyed Severance. I enjoyed it as a filmmaker. I was just blown away at the filmmaking. I was intrigued with the story and the characters. And I think as someone who's worked in corporate America, when you understand that it's basically critique and commentary about the modern workplace. (01:30:35): There were times that I just thought were unbelievably funny and insightful. It was definitely interesting watching it with my wife who was an attorney and hasn't worked in those kinds of environments. So it was like an episode where some people got disappeared and the language that we're using was all around the language you would hear around a layoff. (01:30:50): And so I was laughing myself to death, but she was like, "What? What's going on?" So that's super fascinating and then I'll throw one other in there, which is not something I've recently seen, but something I highly recommend for everybody, which is Lords of Arabia. The Lords of Arabia is I think one of the two or three best expressions of the medium of film. (01:31:11): And so when you think about the ability to hold moving pictures, characters, story, music, photography, set design, costume, the whole constellation of variables that come to play into a movie, I think Lords of Arabia is probably one of the two or three most complete expressions of what the medium is capable of. (01:31:30): And I think it's useful to think about in technology, all the different elements of a product and all the different elements of a user interface and how you can break those down the way you can break down all these elements of a movie and how many pieces of software do we use where somebody is actually conducting that symphony in a really coherent, powerful, full on way.
turns.zh: 嗯，我真的很喜欢《脱离》这部剧。作为一名电影制作人，我对它的制作水准赞叹不已。故事和角色也让我深深着迷。作为在美国企业界工作过的人，我深知这部剧是对现代职场的深刻批判和讽刺。（01:30:35）剧中有些情节简直爆笑又富有洞察力。和身为律师却从未在那样的环境中工作过的妻子一起观看时，她完全听不懂那些关于裁员的术语，而我却笑得不行。（01:30:50）这太有趣了。另外，我还要推荐一部近期看过的佳作——《阿拉伯君主》。《阿拉伯君主》堪称电影艺术的巅峰之作之一。当你思考如何在一部电影中完美融合动态画面、角色塑造、故事情节、音乐、摄影、布景设计、服装设计等诸多元素时，《阿拉伯君主》无疑是电影艺术最完整的诠释之一。（01:31:11）这对科技产品设计也同样适用——思考一款产品的各个组件、用户界面的各个元素时，我们会发现，这些元素就像电影的各个构成部分一样，需要以同样的逻辑将其拆解成各个单元。我们日常使用的许多软件，其开发者也像在指挥一场交响乐般，将各个模块完美编排成一个连贯、强劲且完整的系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that movie. Next question, do you have a favorite product that you have recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 我超爱那部电影。下一个问题，你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Bob Baxley
turns.en: You're focused on recent and I'm just going to push back. No, there's nothing terribly recent. The stuff that I go back to, I'll give you a couple of nerdy ones. I have a Leica M6 cam, which is a film camera, and I recently started shooting with film again, which I absolutely love because it forces me to slow down. (01:32:14): I always talk about Leica cameras, they're obscenely expensive, but the thing about Leica cameras is you show up different when you shoot with a Leica. So when people think about cameras, they think about the quality of the image, they don't think about how the tool is going to change them. (01:32:28): When you show up with an iPhone, you're thinking about sharing. When you show up with a film camera, you're thinking about saving film and you're spending more time composing and thinking exactly about the shot. When you show up with a digital SLR, you just take a whole bunch of pictures and hope something's going to turn out. (01:32:42): And so I think these cameras are very useful metaphor for being conscious about how the tools you pick are going to impact the thing that you produce. So once you go into Figma, you've made a decision about the thing you're going to produce. If you stay in a sketchbook, you've made a different decision. If you go into something else, you've made a different kind of decision. (01:33:03): So I say the Leica M6 with film because of that. And then the software product I would point out, which is not terribly new, but I think it's worth noting, is a tool called Habitica. And Habitica is really fascinating. Ultimately, it's a habit tracker and task management app, but it's fundamentally a game. (01:33:21): It's a role playing game where you create a character and your character revolves and can buy armor and go on quests and things as you check off your habits and stuff. And it is the most interesting expression of shifting conceptual models that I've ever seen. (01:33:35): So if you think about a conceptual model, it's sort of the software equivalent of a genre in a movie. And so once you say it's a project management software, you're in a certain genre. If you say it's a productivity tool, you're in a certain genre. So if it's social media, you're in a certain genre. So these are different genres. (01:33:50): And Habitica is really interesting because it mixes genres, it mixes role playing game with to do manager. And so I think it's a really powerful example of how you can really shift the user's thinking in the same way movies for example. Star Wars is ultimately a cowboy movie set in space. (01:34:07): And when you come to those two genre mashups are really interesting. When you come to a rom-com, you have a certain expectation of what's going to happen to a rom-com. If somebody suddenly got shot in a rom-com, that would not make sense to you in the same way that if somebody made a really funny joke in a John Wick movie, it wouldn't make sense. (01:34:23): So I think Habitica is just the most interesting example I've ever found is somebody really doing a fascinating mashup of conceptual models, which is... Sorry, I'll stop. It's an unexplored and unexploited possibility of software ideas.
turns.zh: 你关注的是近期情况，而我只想反驳一下。不，近期的情况其实并不多。让我给你举几个有点书呆子气的例子。我有一台徕卡M6相机，这是一款胶片相机，最近我又开始用胶片拍摄了，因为它能迫使我放慢脚步。（01:32:14）：我总是在谈论徕卡相机，它们贵得离谱，但用徕卡相机拍照会让你显得与众不同。当人们想到相机时，他们首先想到的是图像质量，而非相机工具如何改变自身的创作方式。（01:32:28）：用iPhone拍照时，人们会想着分享照片；用胶片相机拍照时，人们会想着节省胶片，更用心构图，仔细考虑每张照片的取景；用数码单反相机拍照时，人们只是拍个不停，祈祷能拍出好照片。（01:32:42）：所以我认为这些相机是很好的隐喻，提醒我们选择工具会如何影响最终的创作成果。同样，一旦你进入Figma设计平台，你就已经决定了要创作怎样的作品；如果你停留在草稿本阶段，又做出了不同的选择；如果你转向其他工具，也是在做出不同的决定。（01:33:03）：所以我之所以提到徕卡M6相机和胶片摄影，是因为它们能迫使你放慢脚步，专注于创作过程。接下来我想提到的软件产品Habitica，虽然不算最新，但值得一提。这款游戏化习惯管理应用极具魅力。本质上，它是一个角色扮演游戏，你可以创建一个虚拟角色，通过完成习惯任务来升级角色，购买装备、参与任务等。这是我见过最有趣的概念模型转换案例。（01:33:35）：如果你思考一个概念模型，它相当于软件领域的电影类型。当你说这是一款项目管理软件时，就属于某个类型；说它是生产力工具，又属于另一个类型；如果是社交媒体应用，则是完全不同的类型。（01:33:50）：Habitica尤其有趣，它将不同类型融合在一起，将角色扮演游戏与任务管理器相结合。我认为这是一个强有力的例子，展示了如何像电影一样重塑用户思维。例如，《星球大战》本质上是太空西部片。（01:34:07）：当两种类型相融合时，效果往往令人惊喜。比如浪漫喜剧片，你对其情节走向有固定预期；但若浪漫喜剧片中突然出现枪战桥段，你会觉得突兀，就像在《疾速追杀》电影中听到搞笑笑话一样令人不适。（01:34:23）：所以我认为Habitica是我见过最有趣的案例，它成功地将不同概念模型进行了令人惊叹的融合，这……抱歉，我要打住了。软件创意领域还有许多未被探索和开发的可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how profound this lightning round already is. The point about Leica changing the way you even think about the photo is so interesting, I've never thought of it that way. You mentioned Star Wars. Have you seen Andor by the way?
turns.zh: 这场闪电问答环节已经如此深刻，真是令人惊叹。关于徕卡改变人们对摄影看法的观点太有意思了，我从未这样想过。您提到《星球大战》。对了，您看过《安多》吗？
